policies.statement: Support Māori autonomy in their responses to climate change

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that the overarching legislation for addressing climate change is too weak to actually prevent the negative impacts we are seeing and will see more in the future. Large, profit-driven corporations are influencing decision-makers reducing the voice of individuals and communities. NZ's dependence on fossil fuel is also deeply embedded in all parts of our economy, which is a barrier to economic resilience and limits the effectiveness of climate policies.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value:
This party would require the implementation of Te Tiriti o Waitangi and co-governance in decision-making and extend the Climate Change Response Act to cover every sector and all greenhouse gases. 
Domestic air and shipping fuel emissions would also be included in calculating emissions for both the public and private sectors. Non-forestry carbon sequestration technologies would be on a pathway to net carbon-zero, and emission reduction targets would be transparent and align with global obligations. Purchases of offshore emissions credits would be allowed only as a last resort. There would be robust monitoring and enforcement of the legal obligations for emissions reduction contained in the Act.

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that all sectors need to be incentivised to reduce their greenhouse gas emissions, in order to prioritise the health of the environment and humanity over profit.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would phase out the free allocation of NZUs to emission-Intensive and trade-exposed industries, and implement a framework for pricing agricultural greenhouse gas emissions. It would also include emissions from international aviation in pricing schemes. Marine-based 'blue carbon' - carbon dioxide captured and stored by the world's ocean and coastal ecosystems - would be included in the ETS. Alternative emissions pricing mechanisms would be implemented when the ETS is not doing its job in reducing greenhouse gas emissions. Lastly, existing foresters would received equitable treatment from any changes in forestry-related carbon offsetting systems.

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that that New Zealand has a legal and moral responsibility, supported by the Te Tiriti o Waitangi, to lead climate action on a global scale. New Zealand is relatively wealthy but currently ranks poorly against other countries for its climate change policies. This party says we need to do better to help our vulnerable neighbours, like Pacific Island nations.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would advocate internationally for the strengthening of international climate agreements and encourage all countries to increase their Nationally Determined Contributions so that global emissions halve by 2030 and reach net carbon-negative by 2050 to limit global average temperature rise to 1.5 degrees Celsius. The party would also advocate for urgent climate action to be embedded in all international agreements and institutions, with a legally binding mechanism created to ensure international compliance with climate commitments and ramped-up funding made available to finance climate adaptation around the world. It would promote that decisions are led by Indigenous leadership and countries and communities particularly vulnerable to climate change.

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that drugs exist and people use them. This party wants to reduce harm that can arise from drug use by taking a health-based approach rather than a punitive approach to drug use. Drug criminalisation leads to unsafe drug use, fosters organised crime, and traps those convicted in a cycle of poverty that, in turn, contributes to harmful drug use.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would repeal and replace the Misuse of Drugs Act with an evidence-based approach that reduces harm, treats drug use as a health issue and provides for regulated access to cannabis for personal use. As a short-term measure, it would implement the recommendations of the Law Commission’s 2011 review of the Misuse of Drugs Act 1975. The new Act would be co-designed with Māori under a Te Tiriti o Waitangi framework and would promote the rights and interests of whānau, hapū, and iwi.

attributes.value:

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that te Tiriti must be upheld as the fundamental document that the Treaty of Waitangi Act is based on. In its view, successive governments have consistently breached Te Tiriti, eroding the true partnership that was intended. Te Tiriti o Waitangi references have recently been weakened or stripped out of 19 acts of Parliament. And in government decision-making, iwi and hapū are often treated as advisors, rather than the partners which they are meant to be.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value:
This party would amend the Treaty of Waitangi Act so Te Tiriti is the authoritative text. It would implement genuine Te Tiriti decision-making models across government, and ensure iwi and hapu are resourced to participate as partners.
It would increase resourcing for the Waitangi Tribunal and give it the power to make binding recommendations for the return of Crown and private land. 
It would facilitate the return of whenua outside of Treaty Settlements that was wrongfully alienated from tangata whenua, including a possible right-of-first-refusal process at point of sale. It would also reform the Treaty Settlements process to enable fair negotiations and just reparations without cessation of sovereignty.

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that small businesses are facing an economy that is stacked against them. Liquidations are the highest in almost 15 years and a lack of supermarket competition is squeezing shoppers and local suppliers. International corporates are flourishing while factories close and local businesses struggle. This party will work for an even playing field for local businesses and support sustainable low-carbon industries.

attributes.value: This party would encourage consumer to support local by revitalising ‘Buy Kiwi Made’ and expanding country of origin labelling; commit government departments to buying more NZ goods and services; reform competition laws to create a fairer playing field for small businesses and consumers. It would foster sustainable, low carbon jobs in the ICT sector, particularly smaller firms. And it would invest in community-led regional development with a focus on sustainable building, regenerative agriculture, low-carbon infrastructure and iwi/hapū led economic activity.

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that seniors have cared for us and many continue to do so during retirement. They should feel valued, connected and able to live with dignity. The says that, additionally, there should also be more support for the conditions and pay of aged care workers.

attributes.value: This party would launch a long‑term seniors strategy that addresses kaumātua wellbeing, elder abuse, equitable incomes, and the creation of a state‑owned, not‑for‑profit retirement village system. It would boost funding for senior community spaces and activities, expand housing options such as papakāinga and address social housing waitlists for kaumātua. It would support warm, accessible, smaller home designs and back fair pay and conditions for aged care workers.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would transfer responsibility of local elections to the Electoral Commission. Sixteen year olds would be allowed to vote in local elections and all councils would use a Single Transferable Vote (STV) system. To enhance democracy and community input, councils could use tools like citizens assemblies to make decisions, especially regarding reorganisation of council bodies.

Councils would be allowed to reinstate Māori wards. attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would reject the proposed rates cap where councils could only increase rates between 2 and 4 percent annually. Councils could set rates as they chose. Councils would also be allowed to use bed levies, congestion charging and charge GST on rates and other growth.

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that people experiencing mental distress deserve access to care, no matter where they are. Social factors like the climate crisis, poverty and unemployment exacerbate the mental health crisis in NZ. Mental health services should be well funded and integrated into the public health system, not fragmented and requiring people to turn to private services which also have long waiting lists. Harmful practices, like seclusion, should be phased out so that care does not cause further harm

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would extend free mental health care to all communities, with more funding for community-specific mental health care. This includes youth services like Piki, Mana Ake and Youth One Stop Shops throughout Aotearoa. It also includes Asian Family Services and dedicated support for postnatal mental health. Mental health facilities would be further resourced so that the practice of seclusion could be phased out, replaced by community care models. Specific kaupapa Māori mental health and addiction programmes, including programmes focused on youth, would be funded as well.

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that AI data centres can currently be consented by councils with no community input. Overseas, data centres have had adverse effects on local water supplies and are high energy users, driving up power prices. The Datagrid data centre in Southland is expected to use 6 per cent of the country's electricity supply. This party says there needs to be more transparency and a chance for regulation to be developed.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would call for a one-year moratorium on new AI data centres while proper rules are put in place to ensure there are benefits and don't unduly strain our resources. Solutions could include forcing centres to build their own energy or use closed loop water cooling systems, but currently there are no requirements for these under NZ rules.

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that data is a taonga (treasure). The party believes that New Zealanders, iwi, hapū, communities, and creators should retain meaningful control over how data about them is used. Language in particular is crucial to identity and culture, and must be protected from AI.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would enforce explicit consent standards for AI training data, where appropriate remuneration must be provided for any Intellectual property used for training AI models. The party would ensure there are fines for any breaches, with the Privacy Commissioner given more power to enforce NZ's privacy laws. Government AI systems would be transparent, and there would be specific regulations requiring co-governance and co-development of Māori data and IP to protect Māori data sovereignty. Lastly, private information provided to the government and classified government will not be sent to third parties for model training.

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that while AI seems like a virtual technology, it actually consumes large amounts of resources, taking up land, using water to cool servers and requiring electricity to power data centres. This party says that any data centres based in New Zealand would need to follow strict regulations to protect the environment.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would require AI data centres to report on their environmental impact before being built. New facilities would be required to provide new renewable energy to cover their electricity use and their would be community consultation during the consenting process. To increase transparency, this party would require data centres to report their water use publicly.

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that AI companies can concentrate economic power, leading to bad outcomes for workers and individuals. These risks should be regulated by government.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would encourage the use of public-interest and open-source AI models wherever possible, and mandate the use of multiple and interchangeable AI models to prevent vendor lock-in. It would encourage the use of NZ-based and NZ-focussed large language models, rather than relying on AI tools from overseas companies.

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that AI can concentrate economic power and impact individuals and communities. Power should not be concentrated, and the use of AI should not be at the expense of children and worker's rights.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would ensure children are not forced to use AI, especially at school, and broadly make sure that AI use around kids is in line with the UNCRC’s Joint Statement on Artificial Intelligence and the Rights of the Child. It would also require that workers are consulted about AI use in their workplace.

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that people have a right to know when they are interacting with AI and how it is being used. AI content should always be clearly labelled so that people understand when they are using an AI model.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would create labelling requirements for artificial intelligence, and audit algorithms for high-risk AI systems, so there is monitoring of AI use in the public sector. It would create an AI office within the department of prime minister and cabinet (DPMC) and aim to eventually establish an AI commission with independent powers to conduct audits assurance and education regarding AI use. This party would also collaborate with international best practice like the EU AI Act and build on NZ's work in the Christchurch Call to cooperate with like-minded countries regarding AI regulation and governance.

party.description: The New Zealand Labour Party (Rōpū Reipa o Aotearoa) is a centre-left social democratic party. Its program emphasises the incremental expansion in the role of government in the economy to address poverty and inequality. It currently has 34 seats in parliament. Formed in 1916 by Trade Unions and Socialist political parties, it is historically responsible for much of the modern welfare system. It has held seats in every Parliament since winning 8 in 1919, forming its first government in 1935. Since then, Labour has formed governments on 6 different occasions. Chris Hipkins is the party leader, and its 2026 slogan is ‘Better Starts Now.”
party.name: Labour Party

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that that last year, 155,000 New Zealanders didn't collect medicine they had been prescribed because they couldn't afford it. Not receiving treatments mean that health problems are exacerbated, and research shows that people who skip medication are more likely to end up in hospital. Making prescriptions free is an upfront cost for the government which removes pressure on the health system.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would remove the $5 fee for prescriptions of funded medication. This would apply to anyone who is entitled to free healthcare in New Zealand, instead of just people under age 14 and over age 65 and those with Community Services Cards. This would cost $74.5m a year, funded by a capital gains tax.  This party estimates that this policy would cost $74.5 m a year.

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that many New Zealanders have to choose between medical care and other essentials like food. Some general practices charge nearly $100 per visit. Under the "Medicard" policy programme, anyone eligible for funded healthcare could go to the GP for free at least three times a year. This would be paid for by a capital gains tax.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would cover three visits a year to a doctor or nurse at the GP clinic where people are enrolled. Already free services like immunisations would not count towards the three-visit total. The "Medicard" card and app would link visits to people's National Health Index number. The three free visits are for each year and do not accumulate and roll over into the next year.  This party estimates that this policy would cost $393.3 million in 2027/28, rising to around $553 million a year once fully in place.

attributes.value: This party says that NZ is one of the few countries in the world without some form of capital gains tax. Money raised from the tax would be invested in healthcare.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would introduce a 28% tax on commercial properties and residential investment properties. Family farms, homes, KiwiSaver, shares, business assets, inheritances, gifts, and personal items would be exempt. The tax would only apply to people who own multiple properties or commercial properties, and only to profits made after 1 June 2027.

There would be no sign-up required; transport users would use their public transport card or payment method as usual for public buses and trains and some ferries.

attributes.value: This party says that that cervical cancer is one of the most preventable cancers but 85 percent of those diagnosed have never been screened or have missed screenings. Free cervical screening means earlier diagnosis, less pressure on hospitals and more lives saved.

party.description: New Zealand First (Aotearoa Tuatahi) are a centrist, yet socially conservative party. The party has traditionally supported a moderate role for government. It emphasises its ability to be a check on both Labour and National and marry economic moderation with conservative views on gender, indigenous rights and immigration. Led by long-term leader Winston Peters, the party has been in government on four occasions, once with National in 1996, then Labour in 2005 and 2017. It has been in government with National and Act from 2023 to 2026. It is known for introducing the gold card for pensioners in 2008 and supporting extractive industries.
party.name: NZ First

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that New Zealanders are paying too much for power, because four large companies generate 90 percent of NZ's power, controlling the supply and selling the power directly to customers. The party says that this situation results in high prices for households and industry, leading to companies closing down and job losses.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would replace the current system so that generation and retail are not done by the same companies. This would make sure that the most expensive generator would not set the price for the rest of the market.

citations.title: 'Breaking up the Gentailers', undated (accessed 13 August 2026)

policies.statement: Divide the "generation" and "retail" aspects of power companies

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that prices for electricity are too high in NZ. Because of the structure of the market with four major companies, it is hard for competitors to enter the market. The "gentailer" companies can hold back supply, making electricity more expensive, instead of investing in more power generation.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would guarantee long-term, fixed-price contractions for building new electricity generation. The companies building this infrastructure would receive guarantees that their power would be the first to be used when needed. This would make it easier for investors to fund electricity generation projects, and increase New Zealand's energy security and resilience.

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that food prices are too high in New Zealand, as a result of a supermarket duopoly controlling 80% of the grocery market. Food producers and households do not get a good deal from this system. Creating more competition will drive prices down.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would introduce legislation to split the Foodstuffs brands into two cooperatives; one for New World and Four Square and the other for Pak'n'Save. This would create more competition with Woolworths and result in lower prices and fairer deals for producers. This would create more certainty for major businesses like McCains and Heinz Watties, which have experienced job losses as a result of a poorly functioning system.

attributes.name: Why

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would increase the powers assigned to the Commerce Commission and Grocery Commissioner. The Commerce Commission would be able to apply penalties for serious breaches of up to $10 million, three times the gain, or 10 percent of turnover. Investigations would be faster and enforcement stricter. The Grocery Commissioner would have powers to investigate, make binding decisions and apply penalties directly.

attributes.name: Why

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that NZ needs to gain the maximum benefit from its resources. Knowing which resources are available is a key step for making decisions about future mining projects. Investing in science, technology and the mining workforce will protect the benefits of mining into the future.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would invest in advanced core-scanning technology and pay for a modern geological survey to be done throughout NZ. It would also reopen the School of Mines to build the mining workforce and ensure that money made in the mining industry stays in NZ. Building on policies like Fast-track, this would make it easier for new mines to be created.

citations.title: 'Returning 50% of mining royalties to the regions', undated (accessed 13 August 2026)

policies.statement: Survey all of NZ to look for minerals

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that 85 percent of New Zealand banks are owned by Australian companies, and lending is offered at margins higher than Australia. Domestically-owned Kiwibank has just 8 percent of the mortgage market. A New Zealand bank of a similar scale would compete with these major Australian banks and promote economic sovereignty.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would use ACC, banking bonds, Crown debt and Kiwisaver capital to buy BNZ from the National Australia Bank. It would be combined with Kiwibank to form the fully Crown-owned National Bank of New Zealand. The profits generated by BNZ would finance the buy-back.

citations.title: 'Backing a New Zealand Owned Bank', undated (accessed 13 August 2026)

policies.statement: Return BNZ to NZ ownership

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that ensuring children are enrolled in Kiwisaver would create benefits that compound for decades. Birth enrollment ensures that all New Zealanders can participate, and an up-front government contribution of $1,000 would mean that all citizens will enter adulthood with savings.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would enrol all New Zealand citizens in Kiwisaver at birth and provide a $1,000 contribution to all these accounts from the Crown. This would complement other Kiwisaver policies, including increasing employee and employer contribution to 8% and 10% and making enrolment compulsory for all people in the workforce.

citations.title: 'Establishing a Kiwisaver Generation', undated (accessed 13 August 2026)

policies.statement: Enrol New Zealand citizens in Kiwisaver at birth

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that this board is not accountable to ratepayers, yet influences decisions that are part of Auckland Council. The board is not elected and cost $3.5m last year. It says that Auckland Council can engage with Māori and recognise their interests but that this engagement should happen through people who are elected.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would introduce a members bill to disestablish the Independent Māori Statutory Board. All functions of the board would be returned to the main body of Auckland Council.

citations.title: 'Disestablish Auckland's 'Independent Maori Statutory Board'', undated (accessed 13 August 2026)

policies.statement: Disestablish the Independent Māori Statutory Board from Auckland Council

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that New Zealand's birth rate is only 1.53 children per woman, when the replacement rate is 2.1 children per woman. If something is not done, this party says New Zealand may become entirely dependent on immigration in the future.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would offer all new parents (where at least one is a New Zealand citizen) a $5000 grant per year for the first three years of their child's life. This grant would apply to the first, second, and third children which the couple have. The grant would be tax free and not replace any current support.  This party estimates that this policy would cost $400 million per three-year-cycle.

citations.title: 'The 'Kiwi Kids Grant'', undated (accessed 13 August 2026)

policies.statement: Support new parents with a $5000 grant for the first three years of their child's life

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value:
This party says that the present 50 million litres per year is too low to incentivise production at a large scale. The status-quo supports New Zealand-based dairy manufacturers, but does not support these firms to scale to size, which disincentives investment into Fonterra. 

Marketing ‘New Zealand Dairy’, this party sees this policy as a means of making NZ’s dairy manufacturing sector more competitive in export markets. It says it is important for the milk provision not to be a subsidy; dairy manufacturing firms would cover delivery and collection costs and pay farmers market rates.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would increase milk access from 50 million litres to 500 million litres per year over the first six years. From there, access would taper to 80 per cent, 60 per cent, 40 per cent and 20 per cent to encourage immediate investment. This would be done through changing the Dairy Industry Restructuring Act 2001.

citations.title: 'NZ First launches 'Use It or Lose It' dairy policy', 20 August 2026 (accessed 26 August 2026)

policies.statement: Increase the milk quantity guaranteed to NZ dairy manufacturing

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says Marsden Point should be allowed to operate under a lighter regulatory framework to support domestic energy production. The party argues that, with rising global tensions and increasing energy costs, New Zealand needs to better ensure itself against spikes in global fuel prices. Establishing a special economic zone (SEZ) will attract foreign investment.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would establish a Special Economic Zone, which would see a combination of tax breaks, wage subsidies, and reduced regulation to incentivise the development of energy and port operations. The party says that the principal benefits of the economic zone would be the bypassing of planning regulations and the RMA. If elected, this party would consider providing additional funding to help local councils run services in the SEZ, such as investment in physical, transport or communications infrastructure.

citations.title: 'Establishing a Special Economic Zone At Marsden Point', undated (accessed 13 August 2026)

policies.statement: Establish a Special Economic Zone at Marsden Point

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party claims the rebuild is representative of Christchurch's earthquake recovery. Completing the rebuild would restore a symbol of the city's heritage and be a boost for local tourism and business in the city.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value:
The party has pledged $15m dollars to Christ Church Cathedral Reinstatement Ltd to complete the company's proposed pathway. The funding would be alongside money Christchurch City Council, not instead of. 

The additional government funding would help complete the first stage of the new rebuild project. This would re-open the Cathedral and remove the hoardings from the square during the first stage of full revitalisation.

 This party estimates that this policy would cost 15 million over one year.

citations.title: 'Complete the Christchurch Cathedral', undated (accessed 13 August 2026)
'NZ First Campaign Announcement: Funding For Christ Church Cathedral Rebuild', 27 March 2026 (accessed 27 August 2026)

policies.statement: Complete the reconstruction of Christchurch Cathedral

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that Māori have been better represented since the establishment of MMP. When MMP was introduced, a report recommended scrapping the old Māori seats because Māori would be better represented. The party argues that a referendum is needed to justify the seats' existence and so the issue can be settled. It also cites the conduct of Te Pati Māori in Parliament as justifying the need for a referendum.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would introduce legislation to run a public referendum on the Māori seats at the next general election. It says the referendum would have no extra costs if it could be included on the ballot papers at the next general election. The result would not affect the outcomes of that election, but the following election three years later.

citations.title: 'Referendum on Maori Seats', undated (accessed 13 August 2026)

'Referendum on Maori Seats
', undated (accessed 27 August 2026)

policies.statement: Introduce a binding referendum on the Māori seats

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that it is a problem that after two years of living in NZ, someone can claim permanent residency and vote. For visa holders who have no expiry date for their visa, they can technically vote after one year. It says that only those who are natural-born citizens and have sworn allegiance to NZ should be able to vote for who governs the country and in referendums that can change NZ.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value:
This party would restrict voting rights for all referenda and levels of government (including local government) to those with legal citizenship.

Permanent residents will still retain other rights such as the right to live, work, study, and access government support.

citations.title: 'Citizen’s Only Voting', undated (accessed 27 August 2026)

policies.statement: Ensure that only NZ citizens can vote

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: The party says that New Zealanders who have worked since they were teenagers deserve security in retirement. As superannuation becomes harder to pay for as the population ages, it's unfair for people who have lived and worked in the country for a lot less time to receive the same payments.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: The party would phase in the demand that one be a citizen to be eligible for superannuation over three years. It would amend the eligibility criteria to remove access to NZ Super for permanent residents.

citations.title:
'NZFirst Campaign Announcement: NZ Super for Citizens Only
', 6 September 2026 (accessed 11 September 2026)

policies.statement: Provide superannuation only to NZ citizens

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that housing is becoming more expensive and that there's a greater need for social housing. The party claims that it is unjust not to distinguish between a citizen and someone yet to become a citizen when providing a scarce resource like social housing.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would amend legislation to prioritise NZ citizens in the allocation of social housing. Resident class visa holders will retain eligibility to be on the waitlist, but NZ citizens will be fast-tracked up the waitlist for social housing.

citations.title: 'NZ First Announces Immigration Reform Policies', 11 September 2026 (accessed 11 September 2026)

policies.statement: Reserve social housing for NZ citizens first

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that the illegal overstaying of visas by migrants is causing public distrust of the immigration system. However, people have built a life here and are discouraged by bans on re-entering the country if caught and deported.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would provide a 24-month/two-year amnesty whereby, if one chooses to self-deport by leaving the country, they will be eligible to apply to immigrate to NZ legally. Any overstayer caught thereafter will receive a permanent ban from applying. Pacific overstayers will be able to apply for a legal visa right away and stay in NZ.

citations.title: 'NZ First Announces Immigration Reform Policies', 11 September 2026 (accessed 11 September 2026)

policies.statement: Allow a two-year amnesty on overstayers if they self-deport

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that student visa holders compete in the competitive graduate job market and can take jobs from New Zealanders. It stays the intent of international education is for overseas economies to give money to NZ by paying for their education, not to provide automatic work rights and residence pathways. The party also cites broader concern with net numbers of migrants entering New Zealand and sees changes to student visas as a way of reducing net migration and its effect on infrastructure.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would have student visa holders lose their automatic right to work. To be allowed to work, student visa holders would have to fulfil strict conditions to ensure they are not doing work that could be done by NZ citizens. People who have been on student visas and want to transition to another visa would have to leave NZ and reapply for a new visa from overseas.

citations.title: 'NZ First Announces Immigration Reform Policies', 11 September 2026 (accessed 11 September 2026)

policies.statement: Remove automatic work rights from student visas

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that benefit support comes with the rights and responsibilities of being a New Zealander. It wants to prevent the use of benefits by migrants yet to become citizens and to slow down net migration.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would implement a benefit stand-down period of ten years. This period would be in line with the additional changes to citizenship and permanent residency, where the required period to qualify for citizenship would double from five years to a minimum of ten years and from two years to five years for permanent residency.

citations.title: 'NZ First Announces Immigration Reform Policies', 11 September 2026 (accessed 11 September 2026)

policies.statement: Create a benefit stand-down period of ten years for migrants and lengthen residency and citizenship eligibility

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that that public trust in the immigration system requires trust that violent offenders would be deported. Immigration to NZ is a privilege, not a right.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would widen the criteria for deportation liability to cover any offence for which imprisonment is available as a sentence. Automatic deportation will be applied to those found guilty of violent or sexual crimes, fraud, participating in an organised criminal group, money laundering, or exploiting migrants.

citations.title: 'NZ First Announces Immigration Reform Policies', 11 September 2026 (accessed 11 September 2026)

policies.statement: Expand criteria for deportation

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that application fees will be increased to fund the additional administrative burden of its other immigration reforms. Such increases should be accepted by applicants, as, according to the party, immigration to NZ is a privilege, not a right. The party claims that the application fee should be reflective of the value of becoming a New Zealander.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would increase citizenship and permanent residence application fees. The revenue gained from this will fund the additional administrative burden resulting from these stricter processes.

citations.title: 'NZ First Announces Immigration Reform Policies', 11 September 2026 (accessed 11 September 2026)

policies.statement: Raise citizenship and permanent residence application fees

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that too large a share of NZ health spending goes towards caring for people once they're sick, as opposed to before. The party claims that 59% of health spending is spent treating chronic illness, and only 1.75% on the prevention of such conditions.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would promote nutrition from primary school to medical school, use health coaches in GP care, and require a full independent review of our dietary guidelines. It would fund research and development to better assess nutritional interventions for preventing and treating mental illness. It would fund development in agricultural tech and cut regulatory barriers to help grow markets for organic food items.  It would investigate how the use of vitamins in the delivery of healthcare can prevent people from getting sick again, including intravenous vitamin C pre- and post-surgery for preventing and treating infections.

citations.title:
'NZFirst Campaign Announcement: The Plan to “Make NZ Healthy”
', 20 September 2026 (accessed 21 September 2026)

policies.statement: Promote healthy eating as preventative healthcare

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that the healthcare system responds to crises without dealing with the underlying causes, such as poor nutrition. It claims the incorporation of health coaches can help educate patients on how to better avoid underlying causes of illness.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would fund health coaches to be staffed at local general practices.

citations.title:
'NZFirst Campaign Announcement: The Plan to “Make NZ Healthy”
', 20 September 2026 (accessed 21 September 2026)

policies.statement: Make health coaches an integrated part of primary care

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that there is too little investment in preventive care. Poor nutrition is a driver of underlying conditions that lead people to need expensive healthcare.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would fund NZ scientists to assess nutritional interventions for preventing and treating mental illness. It would remove Medsafe/Pharmac barriers to recognising safe nutrients and invest in hospital trials that assess the effectiveness of intravenous vitamin C to treat infections. Farmers would be supported by to invest in the research of alternatives to potentially harmful agricultural sprays. It would fund development in agricultural tech and cut regulatory barriers to help grow markets for organic food items.

citations.title:
'NZFirst Campaign Announcement: The Plan to “Make NZ Healthy”
', 20 September 2026 (accessed 21 September 2026)

policies.statement: Fund organic and nutrient-based health interventions

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that too large a share of NZ health spending goes towards caring for people once they're sick, as opposed to before. The party claims that 59% of health spending is spent treating chronic illness, and only 1.75% is spent on the prevention of such conditions. Better education and info can help inform people of how they can best make healthier decisions.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would launch an independent review that seeks to better understand metabolic health. It would promote nutrition from primary school to medical school. Such a review would look at current dietary guidelines.

citations.title: 'New Zealand First Makes Mill Road Extension A Priority For South Auckland', 17 August 2026 (accessed 24 August 2026)

policies.statement: Commission a full and independent review of NZ's nutritional guidelines and education

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that preventive care is underemphasised as part of the NZ health system. Regulatory barriers can increase costs for doctors, and professional standards are seen as too restrictive from the party's perspective.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would reduce the regulatory burden on doctors in primary care. It would also allow greater diversity of medical viewpoints in professional standards.

citations.title:
'NZFirst Campaign Announcement: The Plan to “Make NZ Healthy”
', 20 September 2026 (accessed 21 September 2026)

policies.statement: Increase autonomy and reduce administration for general practitioners

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that NZ firms need support for greater productivity and growth. The party argues that small businesses operating on thin margins need additional support to invest, develop, and start up.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would lower the corporate tax rate for all firms with turnover less than $30 million. The party claims the cost would initially be $1 billion and that additional growth would cover additional costs over time.

citations.title: 'Lowering Tax Rate for SMEs to 20%', undated (accessed 24 September 2026)

policies.statement: Lower the corporate tax rate to 20% for small businesses

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that the Waitangi Tribunal, in its capacity to hear alleged ongoing breaches of the Treaty, is beginning to violate Parliament's sovereignty and voters' rights through its criticism of government policy.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would replace the Waitangi Tribunal with the Treaty of Waitangi Completion Commission, tasked with finalising all claims lodged before 2008.  It would implement this policy within the first hundred days of forming a government.

citations.title: 'Winston Peters - “Ending the Waitangi Make-Work Industry”', 27 September 2026 (accessed 27 September 2026)
'NZFirst to Campaign on Ending the Waitangi Make-Work Industry', 27 September 2026 (accessed 27 September 2026)

policies.statement: Replace the Waitangi Tribunal with a Treaty of Waitangi Completion Commission

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that the fireworks cause distress for pets, fires, and lead to increased use of emergency response resources. This leads to healthcare and ACC costs.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would introduce legislation that will stop the retail sale, manufacture, and importation of fireworks for public use. Fireworks would still be allowed for approved public displays.

citations.title: 'NZFirst to Ban Public Sales of Fireworks', 9 October 2026 (accessed 09 October 2026)

policies.statement: Ban public sales of fireworks

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that working parents are struggling to get by and afford the essentials. The party cites the additional, but temporary, $50 added to the IWFTC by the government this year as needing to be increased and made permanent. The party says such changes will turn the temporary relief into a long-term pathway for parents in work to be able to plan for their families’ future.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would increase the IWFTC by $70 a week. The increase would not apply to the Family Tax Credit (FTC), which covers parents regardless of employment status. This party estimates that this policy would cost between $500m and $600m annually.

citations.title: 'NZ First to Increase Working for Families, Minimum Wage', 10 October 2026 (accessed 12 October 2026)

policies.statement: Increase In-Work-Family-Tax-Credit by $70 a week

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that workers need their wages to not fall below inflation. The party says it has advocated for this in coalitions before and would do so again.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would try to negotiate that the minimum wage increases agreed in coalition agreements be at least the rate of inflation.

citations.title: 'NZ First to Increase Working for Families, Minimum Wage', 10 October 2026 (accessed 12 October 2026)

policies.statement: Increase the minimum wage in line with inflation

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that NZ's immigration system should be used to manage genuine workforce shortages.  However, it says that instead the accredited employer work visa has too often been used as a means to simply find a preferable candidate and is a risk for the workers themselves, who can find themselves with less protection from exploitation.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would replace the Accredited Employer Work Visa with the shortage-led skilled work visa. Such a visa would be limited to shortages, requiring evidence of attempted NZ recruitment, transparency data, and a wage floor to protect domestic wages. The party also says the reforms should be targeted towards the most needed industries, which would restrict access for other industries that have a larger domestic workforce.

citations.title: 'NZFirst to Scrap Accredited Working Visa Model', 11 October 2026 (accessed 12 October 2026)

policies.statement: Replace the Accredited Employer Work Visa with a shortage-led skilled work visa

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that Coastguard, as an organisation, is funded only 40% by the government. 60% of its funding comes from public donations. The party argues that an essential service needs a more reliable funding model, so the organisation has greater certainty.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would increase Coastguard funding. The party would review the Coastguard’s funding arrangement to lift baseline funding and establish a contracting model to ensure that there's adequate access to capital for critical maintenance and capability investment, improved workforce capability, and volunteer support for training, wear and tear, and call-out support. This party estimates that this policy would cost $12 million a year.

citations.title: 'NZ First to increase funding and support to NZ Coastguard', 15 October 2026 (accessed 15 October 2026)

policies.statement: Increase the funding for the NZ Coastguard

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that they support increasing housing supply, but do not want the increase in housing to come at the expense of the quality of public infrastructure or access to services for those who have already lived in affected communities.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would require fast-track housing developers to detail what infrastructure they need and demonstrate whether the present infrastructure can meet demand and has funding. Local authorities would also be required to provide advice on network capacity and delivery risks.

citations.title: 'NZFirst Policy Announcement: Changes to Fast-Track Residential Approvals', 14 October 2026 (accessed 14 October 2026)

policies.statement: Add infrastructure and service capacity requirements to residential fast-track permissions

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that other countries such as Australia, the UK, the US, the EU, and Canada have imposed trade protections on aluminium. The party says jobs at 9 producers across NZ are at risk.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would reverse the current National Party-aligned Minister of Commerce's decision not to pursue trade protections for NZ-produced aluminium.

citations.title: 'NZ First Will Immediately Reverse This Week’s Decision by the Minister of Consumer Affairs', 17 October 2026 (accessed 17 October 2026)

policies.statement: Impose trade barriers to protect NZ-produced aluminium

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that the coroner's report on the killing of Kain Parsons, in conjunction with concerns of illegal underground fight clubs involved in organised crime, requires expanded regulation of combat sports.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would establish a Combat Sports Commission. This organisation would focus on licensing events and promoters to ensure legality and safety. It would introduce minimum health and medical standards, such as pre-and post-fight medical examinations, attending medical practitioners at all events, mandatory stand-down periods between contests determined by medical professionals, and penalty systems for unsanctioned events. The Commission would partner with Sport NZ to to support legitimate promoters and athletes.

citations.title: 'NZ First Announces Overhaul to Regulate Combat Sports', 15 October 2026 (accessed 17 October 2026)

policies.statement: Establish a combat sport commission

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that traffic wait times are too great between Christchurch and the wider Canterbury region. The party says there are existing rail lines between Christchurch and Dunedin, which are owned by the government and should be delivering for the public.  The party wants the trial to determine a business case for permanent passenger rail.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would commence a 12-month trial of passenger rail across Canterbury, such as Christchurch city to Rolleston and Rangiora. It would also connected Canterbury to Otago with a Christchurch-to-Dunedin service.

citations.title: 'NZFirst Campaign Announcement: Commuter Rail For Christchurch, Reinstate Southerner Train', 18 October 2026 (accessed 19 October 2026)

policies.statement: Establish a 12-month trial for commuter rail in Canterbury and further south

party.description: The New Zealand and Freedom Party is a party with a platform largely consists of conservation policy and opposition to COVID restrictions, vaccines, the use of 1080 and fluoridation of water. It was founded in 2015 by Alan Simmons, formerly of the United Future party, and David Haynes, president of the Association of Freshwater Anglers. Following the 2020 pandemic response, many members from the Ban 1080 party joined NZOF. Ban 1080 activist and lawyer Sue Grey is now the elected leader of the party. In 2023, it was part of the wider Freedoms NZ umbrella party, and received 13,025 votes and 0.45% percent of the vote.
party.name: NZ Outdoors & Freedom Party

party.description: The New Zealand National Party (Rōpū Nāhinara) is a centre-right conservative party. It was founded in 1936 as a merger between the liberal United party and conservative Reform parties, its programmes have emphasised the incremental reduction in the role of government to support business and encourage growth. It currently leads the government with 49 seats in parliament. National has historically been regarded as the ‘natural party of government.’ Having been dominant throughout the 20th century.  It has led the government 6 times and held office for longer than Labour. Christopher Luxon is the current leader, with a 2026 slogan of “Fixing the Basics, Building the Future.”
party.name: National Party

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that Rolleston is a well-placed hub for moving goods around, as it is on State Highway 1, the main southern train line, and connected by road and rail to the West Coast. Because many agricultural goods are moved through this area, making it easier to move goods between trains and trucks will increase efficiency and economic opportunity for producers in this area.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would invest $50m in a road and rail "intermodal hub" in Rolleston. This funding would be dependent on the result of a business case, where private freight companies and customers would also invest in the hub. It would only go ahead with a mix of public and private funding.  This party estimates that this policy would cost $50m.

citations.title: 'National's plan for the South Island' (PDF), 14 August 2026 (accessed 18 August 2026)
'National Backs South Island Growth', 14 August 2026 (accessed 18 August 2026)

policies.statement: Invest $50m in roads and rail lines to create a transport hub in Rolleston

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that Queenstown is growing fast and there is a lot of traffic on the section of road between Hansen Road down to the Five Mile roundabout. This party says this road should be wider, as it carries freight, tourists and workers. The gondola, which reduces traffic as well as being a tourist attraction and the local government should receive funding for it as public transport.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would commit $25m to increasing the section of State Highway 6 in Queenstown to four lanes. It would also ensure that the Queenstown gondola could access money from the National Land Transport Fund as a public transport service.

citations.title: 'National Backs South Island Growth', 14 August 2026 (accessed 18 August 2026)
'National's plan for the South Island' (PDF), 14 August 2026 (accessed 18 August 2026)

policies.statement: Widen State Highway 6 in Queenstown and allow the Queenstown Gondola to use public transport funding

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that the South Island is particularly vulnerable to failures in transport networks, particularly given its reliance on several bridges. Earthquakes, flooding, spread-out communities, big rivers and mountains all mean roads and bridges can easily be damaged and communities could face long detours or have no way to get around. Focusing government money on improving the most at-risk parts of the network could make the South Island transport network more resilient.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would use the next government policy statement on transport to prioritise the South Island road network's most important points, especially state highway bridges.

citations.title: 'National's plan for the South Island' (PDF), 14 August 2026 (accessed 18 August 2026)
'National Backs South Island Growth', 14 August 2026 (accessed 18 August 2026)

policies.statement: Improve transport links in the South Island, especially state highway bridges

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that the Crown owns 1.2 million hectares of land through the South Island, which is leased to farmers for pastoral grazing. Much of this land is at higher elevations. Farmers need certainty about which kinds of activities they can do on this land without requiring consent. Giving farmers other income sources on this land, like beekeeping or horticulture, would provide farmers with the confidence to invest and diversify.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would pass a law implementing changed policy settings for the kinds of activity to be carried out on Crown pastoral land, and for when farmers need approval or consent for activities.

citations.title: 'National's plan for the South Island' (PDF), 14 August 2026 (accessed 18 August 2026)
'National Backs South Island Growth', 14 August 2026 (accessed 18 August 2026)
'Unlocking Economic Potential on High Country Farms', 2 April 2026 (accessed 19 August 2026)

policies.statement: Change the policy settings for farmers leasing high country land from the Crown

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that international tourists are key parts of the economy, especially those who want to see natural attractions. These are managed by the Department of Conservation, and while New Zealanders could continue accessing them for free, tourists should pay some costs towards the upkeep. This money would be invested into tourist infrastructure at these locations.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would charge international visitors for access to a handful of key NZ attractions from 2027. This money would be largely reinvested in tourist infrastructure and conservation efforts in these areas. This is expected to raise $60 million per year.

citations.title: 'National Backs South Island Growth', 14 August 2026 (accessed 18 August 2026)
'National's plan for the South Island' (PDF), 14 August 2026 (accessed 18 August 2026)
'Landmark Conservation Reform Bill will boost economy and protect nature', 7 May 2026 (accessed 19 August 2026)

policies.statement: Charge international visitors to access locations like Milford Sound, Aoraki, Cathedral Cove and the Tongariro Crossing

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that smaller towns which receive a lot of visitors can have planning rules which make it hard for new businesses to set up. Changing planning rules for town centres would make it easier to convert spaces into new businesses or accommodation. This would especially help places where businesses want to cater to a growing tourist sector.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would create standardised zoning and planning provisions in small towns, aimed at increasing mixed-use buildings and growth in town centres.

citations.title: 'National Backs South Island Growth', 14 August 2026 (accessed 18 August 2026)
'National's plan for the South Island' (PDF), 14 August 2026 (accessed 18 August 2026)

policies.statement: Create standard planning rules for small towns

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that tourism on conservation land is important to the New Zealand economy. More businesses should be able to receive concessions for operations on conservation land, and these concessions should be faster and simpler. This will create jobs and encourage tourists. Currently, around 1,600 businesses operate on conservation land, with revenue around $5.3m each year.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would remove some rules around concessions on conservation land, so 30-40 percent of applications could be processed automatically. Regional performance metrics would calculate how these concessions are granted and how long it takes.

policies.statement: Create timeframes and regional performance metrics for businesses on conservation land

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that rocks from quarrying are useful on farms for tracks and maintenance, but it can be complicated to get consent for this quarrying. Gravel in riverbeds can be used for aggregate, and removing gravel can reduce flood impacts. In the legislation replacing the RMA, consistent rules for this activity will be applied throughout the country.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would create a National Standard for on-farm quarrying and gravel removal from rivers in the legislation replacing the RMA. This would cut consents for farmers and provide sources of gravel and rock.

citations.title: 'National Backs South Island Growth', 14 August 2026 (accessed 18 August 2026)
'National's plan for the South Island' (PDF), 14 August 2026 (accessed 18 August 2026)

policies.statement: Create national standards for quarrying on farms and taking gravel from rivers

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that mining, especially for gold and coal, is an important part of regional economies in Otago and the West Coast of the South Island. Gold export revenues have nearly tripled in the last three years to $1.8bn. Mining projects in the South Island were included in the government's Fast-track approvals law, and a policy statement for mining specifically would emphasise that these projects are important to national exports.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would write a government policy statement on mining and the extractive industries, ensuring these businesses can access the fast-track process.

citations.title: 'National Backs South Island Growth', 14 August 2026 (accessed 18 August 2026)
'National's plan for the South Island' (PDF), 14 August 2026 (accessed 18 August 2026)

policies.statement: Create a policy statement for mining and extraction under the Fast-track Approvals Act

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that data centres are a growing industry well-suited to setting up in NZ, especially the South Island with its cool climate. However, data centres also use a lot of electricity, which could drive up prices for households and businesses. Making sure that data centres are only built when new electricity generation will also be built would give data centres and electricity generators security without making power prices more expensive.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would only approve new data centres when these are accompanied by new, firm generation.

policies.statement: Approve data centres only when they are accompanied by more power production

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that public money should be saved for what is most important, including health infrastructure. Christchurch has the South Island's largest hospital, and the area is growing, so the hospital needs to be larger to meet demand.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would pay for finishing the fit-out of the new wing of Christchurch Hospital. The 96 beds the wing has capacity would be finished and ready for patients, which is estimated to cost $70m.

policies.statement: Complete construction of Tower Three at Christchurch Hospital

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that parts of the South Island are rapidly increasing in population, like Selwyn district and Queenstown. Other places have schools with aging buildings that need to be replaced, like Invercargill and Twizel.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would deliver on 98 new teaching spaces (in addition to 224 already funded), and nearly 100 more classrooms promised for the South Island.

citations.title: 'National Backs South Island Growth', 14 August 2026 (accessed 18 August 2026)
'National's plan for the South Island' (PDF), 14 August 2026 (accessed 18 August 2026)

policies.statement: Deliver 98 new teaching spaces in the South Island

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that the offenders need to face consequences, and building more beds in Christchurch Prison is required so more people face consequences in prison.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would complete the already-agreed redevelopment of Christchurch Men's Prison, increasing the number of beds from 926 to 1166. A health centre and 52 specialist mental health beds are included as part of the plan. This policy would be paid for by a public-private partnership. The first phase would be completed in mid-2030 and is expected to cost $700m-$800m. This party estimates that this policy would cost $700m-$800m..

citations.title: 'National's plan for the South Island' (PDF), 14 August 2026 (accessed 18 August 2026)

policies.statement: Add 240 beds to Christchurch Men's Prison

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that trained and certified service dogs support people with disabilities including blindness and low vision, epilepsy and hearing loss. These animals have the right to access all public places but are sometimes turned away because they are assumed to be pets. An ID card for these animals will ensure that the dogs and their owners can show they have the right to access public places.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would issue a standardised national card for all owners of certified service dogs. This would make it clear to businesses and other operators that these animals and their owners have the right to be in public places, and would distinguish them from other animals and pets which do not have the same rights.

citations.title: 'Service dog IDs to improve disability access', 5 August 2026 (accessed 18 August 2026)

policies.statement: Create an ID card for service dogs to access public places

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that responsibilities for introduced animals are shared between different agencies, which can make management unclear. Species which hunters and anglers appreciate, like trout and deer, are seen only as pests rather than natural resources. Introduced animals should not be seen as pests by default, especially when they are valued for their cultural, economic or caloric potential. It is possible to balance protecting native species and environments and retaining deer to hunt.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would replace the current "Tahr Control Plan" and seek proposals to recognise further "Herds of Special Interest". Introduced species would be recognised in the law, not just as pests.

citations.title: 'National backs hunters and anglers', 25 July 2026 (accessed 18 August 2026)
'National's Plan for Hunting and Fishing' (PDF), undated (accessed 18 August 2026)

policies.statement: Recognise introduced game species in law

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that the Game Council and Fish and Game are run by hunters and anglers, who should take the lead in managing introduced species in their areas. These organisations need a clearly defined role for managing Herds of Special Interest and coordinating access for hunters on conservation land

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would make the Game Council the statutory manager of introduced game animals in NZ. It would also be responsible for managing access for hunting on conservation land and negotiating between the needs of different users. The legislation for Fish and Game New Zealand would be reformed, directing more resources to habitats, accountability for licence holders and simplifying administration.

citations.title: 'National backs hunters and anglers', 25 July 2026 (accessed 18 August 2026)

policies.statement: Make the Game Council and Fish and Game responsible for managing introduced animals

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that hunting can contribute to the economy. People want to come to New Zealand to hunt animals like tahr which cannot be hunted elsewhere. Jobs like taxidermy, guides and helicopters are supported by people hunting. Increasing the number of people coming to New Zealand to hunt will be good for the economy.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would promote tourism for guided hunting in overseas markets. It would simplify the process of shipping a taxidermied trophy animal outside of the country, including working on customs processes and veterinary certification. It would develop further rules around different types of hunting: recreational, commercial, guided, and aerial.

citations.title: 'National's Plan for Hunting and Fishing' (PDF), undated (accessed 18 August 2026)
'National backs hunters and anglers', 25 July 2026 (accessed 18 August 2026)

policies.statement: Promote hunting-related jobs and tourism

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that accessing the outdoors is important for hunting to take place. The current government has created an access charter for recreational hunting and fishing. This party wants to continue that work by adding more hunting-interest groups to the charter and making more Crown-owned land accessible for hunting and fishing.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would add the Game Animal Council, Overseas Investment Office and Land Information NZ to the Access Charter. It would allow hunting on Crown land used by LINZ and open other Crown Land for more hunting and fishing access. Access on Crown pastoral areas would remain the same. Access for hunters would be protected when land is purchased by overseas investors if possible.

citations.title: 'National's Plan for Hunting and Fishing' (PDF), undated (accessed 18 August 2026)

policies.statement: Increase access for hunting on conservation land

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that NZ should grow its exports to reach the goal of doubling exports by 2034. The first seven countries identified for trade deals currently only receive $1.8bn of exports from New Zealand, which shows potential for growth.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would pursue trade deals with Brazil, Switzerland, Argentina, Bangladesh, Nigeria, Uruguay and the European Free Trade Association (Iceland, Liechtenstein and Norway). Negotiations with these countries would begin in the next five years. When deals were signed, a second set of deals with South Africa, Turkey, Colombia, Morocco, Sri Lanka and Mauritius would be the next focus.

policies.statement: Pursue trade deals with European, South American, Asian and African countries

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that exports help grow NZ's economy, increasing jobs and wages. If businesses are selling more outside of NZ, more money will return to local communities. Exports have increased from $94.4bn to $114.1bn over the current term of government, and that trajectory should continue.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would continue to support a goal of doubling NZ's export earnings by 2034. This would be done by carrying out at least 23 trade missions in the next term of government, procuring deals with 13 countries identified as candidates for trade agreements, and by securing agreements for supplying essential goods like oil. Digital customs and trade processes would eliminate barriers to trade, and New Zealand Trade and Enterprise would have a sharper mandate to develop export growth.

policies.statement: Double NZ's export earnings by 2034

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that people who live in rural NZ should be able to access health care without travelling a long way. Ultrasounds are useful diagnostic tools, and giving rural-based clinicians the ability to use them will make it easier to decide whether they can be treated locally or need hospital care. Currently, 29% of rural clinicians are paying for PRIME emergency response training themselves; government funding for this program could make it easier for rural health professionals to respond to emergencies.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would invest $2.5m in a ultrasound training programmed called POCUS, aimed at rural doctors and nurses who carry out after-hours care and provide additional funding for rural clinicians to receive PRIME emergency response training. This would train 140 health professionals in ultrasounds and 150 people in emergency response. To increase the workforce in rural health practices, a $6m investment would help rural general practices to get more staff.  This party estimates that this policy would cost $8.5m.

citations.title: 'Backing our frontline rural health workforce', 30 July 2026 (accessed 18 August 2026)

policies.statement: Increase funding for rural doctors and nurses to train in skills for urgent care

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that teachers arrive in schools without classroom experience, impacting learning. The current government has created the Schools Onsite Training Programme so teachers can receive a stipend to spend three days a week in classrooms while training.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would increase the number of places in the Schools Onsite Training Programme to 704 each year by 2028, focusing on subjects and areas with teacher shortages. It would also add 50 places to the Teacher Bonding Scheme, bringing the total to 235, which is aimed at helping schools with staffing challenges to attract more staff.

citations.title: 'School Onsite Training Programme to provide 704 places every year from 2028', 3 August 2026 (accessed 18 August 2026)

policies.statement: Increase places for student teachers to train in schools while studying

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that parents need more flexibility for taking leave, including taking paid leave at the same time as their partner, so they can receive more support if needed. Current arrangements create financial penalties for people who take time off work to care for their children. Both parents should have the opportunity to access parental leave if they choose.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would increase parental leave to 27 weeks in the 2027 budget, with further increases in 2028 and 2029. This leave could be split between parents or shared in overlapping periods. After returning to work, pay for annual leave would be calculated based on yearly salaries, rather than average pay for parents who have earned less due to taking parental leave. This party would also continue contributing to a parent's Kiwisaver while they take paid parental leave. Eventually, this party would aim to increase paid parental leave to 40 weeks.

policies.statement: Increase paid parental leave to 30 weeks by 2029

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that the existing Harbour Bridge in Auckland is a busy corridor, which is needed for $1b of economic activity. This is projected to increase to $3.9b by 2051. Making it easier to get to central Auckland from the north would be good for productivity and increase economic activity. Bridges and tunnels have both been proposed, but detailed information about this project is needed before the government spends billions of dollars on it.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would fund an independent detailed business case of the second Waitematā crossing, led by someone who reports to the ministers for finance, transport, Auckland and cabinet as a whole. Consultation with other major parties will ensure that funding for this project can endure across terms of government.

policies.statement: Fund a detailed business case investigating another route across of the Waitematā Harbour

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that in contexts like apartments or for renters it isn't possible to install traditional solar panels, but small solar set-ups on balconies are an option. After a review found that these systems are safe, this party says that making the regulations for small solar set-ups in NZ simpler will improve reliability and affordability for people. Countries like Germany already have similar rules, which this party says is proof they will work in New Zealand.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would follow the recommendations in the solar regulatory review, to reduce the number of approvals needed for new solar set-ups. It would allow more installers to carry out inspections and making approval times for lines companies shorter, and estimates that the net benefits would be between $28 million and $50 million over 10 years.  This party estimates that this policy would cost $28 million and $50 million over 10 years.

policies.statement: Review policies allowing "plug-in" and small-scale solar panels for renters and apartments

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that limiting government spending and debt is good for the economy and for people. Having clear rules that governments follow when making decisions about spending is a way to protect the NZ economy from global economic effects.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would commit to returning the government to surplus, where revenue is more than debt, by the 2028/29 financial year. Over time, this would reduce the ratio of debt to GDP.

attributes.value: This party says that high debt levels limit what governments can do while in power. Lower debt levels give the government, and the economy, more options if oil prices increase or natural disasters occur.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would reduce the proportion of debt to less than 40% of GDP and commit to keeping it that low.

policies.statement: Keep government debt below 40 percent of GDP

attributes.value: This party says that if the government spends too much, it can cause inflation and increase interest rates. Ensuring the government is a smaller percentage of NZ's overall GDP would reduce the amount spent on debt servicing and improve economic conditions.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would reduce Crown expenditure to around 30 per cent of GDP. This principle would be applied when determining the government budget.

policies.statement: Keep Crown expenditure close to 30 per cent of GDP

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that that previous clean vehicle standards did not strike the balance between emission reductions and affordability, meaning cars were expensive. The current government made short-term changes to make cars cheaper. This party wants to continue a full review of the Clean Vehicle standards, ensuring used cars should be held to a different standard than new vehicles.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would retain the current Clean Vehicle Standards as a review continues. It would set different emission targets for imported used vehicles compared to new vehicles. It would also work with the vehicle industry to ensure the standards work for importers and create target settings to take effect in January 2028.

policies.statement: Review and revise the Clean Vehicle Standard

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that that it is focused on growing the economy and do not want to introduce new taxes. It does not want to make commitments that would involving adding or increasing taxes for any New Zealanders. It says it can invest in government services without changing any parameters on the tax system.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would not introduce any new taxes, including an accomodation levy or "bed tax" for councils receiving a lot of tourists. It would not introduce any specific tax on banks either.

citations.title: 'No New Taxes under National', 23 August 2026 (accessed 24 August 2026)

policies.statement: Introduce no new taxes in the next term of government

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that Kiwisaver is a way for people to build up money for themselves during retirement, and everyone who is working should be part of it. The money in Kiwisaver is also important for providing capital for investments in New Zealand's future, like major projects or infrastructure. Contributions from the government for babies who are automatically enrolled will help the investment grow over time.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would make Kiwisaver compulsory from July 2028 and life combined contribution rates (individuals and employers) to 12% by 2032. For babies, it would contribute a $1500 "Baby Boost" payment to all New Zealanders at birth, automatically enrolling them in Kiwisaver. It would also make other changes to Kiwisaver, including government contributions through paid parental leave and requiring employers to maintain payments for people over the age of 65 who are still working.
