policies.statement: Enrol New Zealand citizens in Kiwisaver at birth

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that NZ needs to grow its housing stock and infrastructure, and the Fast-track planning laws have made it easier for new housing to be built. However, some councils are concerned that there is not appropriate infrastructure, like roads and water systems, to support these new developments. To make it easier for councils, the costs of this new infrastructure should be easy to recover when a new project is approved.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would allow councils to amend their "Development Contribution" policies to recover costs from new developments, including in the six months after an application is granted, rather than costs being locked in at the time of application. For projects in multiple council areas, there would be a mechanism to calculate costs for different territorial authorities. Over time, this system would be replaced with "Development Levies" which would be in place by 2029.

citations.title: 'Improving infrastructure tools for Fast-track', 14 August 2026 (accessed 18 August 2026)

policies.statement: Reform the development contributions system to pay for infrastructure associated with housing projects

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that hunting is an important part of managing introduced species, and hunters need access to firearms ranges for practicing and information about public land so they can pursue species there. Information from the Outdoor Access Commission will make it easier for hunters to do important work in the areas where they are needed.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would establish a pre-existing right to operate for shooting ranges. It would include the Outdoor Access Commission's maps in a new government environmental management system and work with community organisation and DOC to enhance access to conservation land for hunting.

citations.title: 'National's Plan for Hunting and Fishing' (PDF), undated (accessed 18 August 2026)

policies.statement: Increase public access to conservation land and shooting ranges

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that New Zealanders should keep more money, rather than paying taxes, to save money for their own future. Taking home more pay and repaying a student loan over a longer period will give graduates more options for how to spend their money. People who have been educated in New Zealand and are staying to work here should have more money available while starting their careers.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would reduce the annual repayment rate for student loans to 10 percent, from the current rate of 12 percent. Student loans for people in NZ would remain interest-free. People could continue to make additional repayments if they wished. Currently, there are $16.8bn of student loans owed to the government. Because of a slower rate of repayment, this party would write off $283m of student loans in the 2026/27 financial year to make up the loss in value from the interest-free loans.

policies.statement: Reduce the student loan repayment rate to 10 percent

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that many New Zealanders receive a heavily subsidised education, but do not use their skills in NZ. To support people to stay in New Zealand, overseas-based student loan holders who are not making repayments need to be penalised. The Inland Revenue Department (IRD) already has some tools, like charging interest to overseas-based loan holders and monitoring the border for people who have not paid their student loans. More penalties and limits for people who are not paying their student loans would recover more money.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would add another 1 percent of interest for overseas student loan holders. For overseas-based New Zealanders withdrawing their Kiwisaver under the "permanent migration" category, money from Kiwisaver would clear the remaining student loan debt first. IRD would receive $10m of additional funding for student loan recovery and be allowed to register a charge for recovery in another country without getting a court order. As is already the case in Australia, this party would set up an information-sharing agreement to share details of student loan holders with the UK. If elected, this party would also lower the threshold for issuing an arrest order for not repaying a student loan. It estimates that the $10m of enforcement funding would result in at least $15m of recovered money per year.

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that 1 in 3 children between the ages of 13-17 spends more than 5 hours on social media every day. Parents should not be responsible for monitoring what children are seeing alone; social media companies also have a responsibility to make sure kids are safe. Restricting social media use will give parents and teachers more options to look after teenagers and create positive behavioural shifts.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would pass a bill requiring that companies including Instagram, TikTok, Facebook and Snapchat check the age of all users to make sure they are not under 16. These companies would be required to regularly report on risks to children on their platforms, and an online safety regulator would monitor compliance. AI companies and other new technologies would be included in the framework, and platforms which fail to take these measures will be fined, based on a percentage of their annual global revenue.

citations.title: 'Government moves to ban U16s from social media', undated (accessed 26 August 2026)

policies.statement: Ban under-16 year olds from social media

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that median increases of rate around the country have been as much as 14.2 percent in the last year. Paying for rates adds financial pressure to households and limiting the amount that rates can increase by would mean that councils prioritise roads, water systems, rubbish and parks rather than other services.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would limit council rate rises to between 2 and 4 percent per year. Every 6 years, this target range would be reviewed and adapted if necessary. In exceptional circumstances, councils could apply for an exemption by demonstrating their financial management or to recover from an unpredictable event like a natural disaster. An independent regulator would monitor and advise councils and the government on the rates target. The caps would take effect from 1 July 2029.

policies.statement: Instruct councils to keep annual rate increases between 2 and 4 percent

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that fuel excise tax was going to be increased in 2027, after a pause due to high cost of living and fuel. The tax, which has been frozen since 2020, is important for funding road infrastructure. With the conflict in Iran making fuel more expensive, fuel tax and road user charge increases can be delayed a year, until 2028.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would cancel the planned 12c increase to the fuel excise tax in 2027. Instead, the party would increase the fuel excise tax in 2028, rising by 5c at 6 month intervals until 2030. At that point, annual 5c increases would resume. Because the excise tax goes into the National Land Transport Fund for road maintenance and creation, it would make up the shortfall with money from other parts of the government.

policies.statement: Do not increase fuel excise tax and Road User Charges until 2028

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that that the Kiwisaver policy was designed with urban housing in mind. Farm workers may be living in provided housing, and not able to access Kiwisaver for a house, as they are not living in the home. This means that people working on farms have to wait longer to buy property. Similarly, Kiwisaver withdrawals cannot be used for purchasing a farm through a company. This change will allow people to buy their first farms with less debt.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would amend the Kiwisaver legislation to allow people working on farms in provided housing to use their Kiwisaver balance for their first house, even if they are not living in it. If they are buying a farm where they are the majority owner, and will be living on the farm, regardless of whether the ownership structure is a partnership, a trust, a company or individuals, they will be eligible to withdraw their Kiwisaver for this purchase too.

policies.statement: Allow Kiwisaver to be used by farm workers buying homes or farms

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that councils create the infrastructure tourists use and deserve a direct financial benefit for hosting visitors, who also put pressure on local resources. Distributing the international visitor levy money not committed to the Department of Conservation and a tourism growth fund to councils is an alternative to a bed tax, which would disproportionately affect domestic tourists in New Zealand. This would also give councils money sooner than the time it would take to set up a bed fee. This is an alternative to raising taxes, which this party opposes.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would distribute $100m of the International Visitor Levy to DOC and $50m to a Tourism Priorities fund each year. The rest of the money, an estimated $385m over the first four years, would be distributed to councils, determined as a share of how many international visitors spend the night in their areas. This party would also commit to keeping the levy at the current amount for the next three years, to provide certainty to the tourism industry. As tourist numbers grow, the amount given to councils is expected to increase.

citations.title: 'International Visitor Levy reset to keep taxes low', 8 September 2026 (accessed 08 September 2026)
'International Visitor Levy reset to keep taxes low', undated (accessed 10 September 2026)

policies.statement: Distribute money from the international visitor levy directly to councils

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that a home is an essential way for New Zealanders to build wealth. The First Home Loan scheme has operated since 2003, allowing people to purchase their first homes with a 5% deposit, instead of a standard 20% deposit. However, some people who are struggling to afford the deposit on their first home fall above the income cap of $95,000 for a person buying alone and $150,000 for two people buying together (both with no dependents). Raising the eligibility criteria will mean more people can buy homes with low deposits. Raising and simplifying the eligibility will allow more people to buy houses.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would raise the eligibility so anyone earning less than $300,000 per year, whether single or a couple, could access the 5% deposit of the First Home Loan scheme. These lower deposits would only apply to people purchasing their first property. The loans would be approved by banks, as already happens, meaning no-one would be issued with a loan they cannot afford. The fiscal impact of this policy is expected to be between $4m-$6m.

'National’s plan to welcome more Kiwis home
', 13 October 2026 (accessed 13 October 2026)

policies.statement: Raise the income threshold for people who can pay a lower deposit for their first home

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that home energy tools like solar power and batteries lower household power bills and provide resilience in the energy system. Electrification and renewable energy is a good investment, and a government backed fund will make it easier for people to add these developments to their homes or businesses. With a high cost of living, this would help people finding it hard to pay power bills.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would launch the Home Energy Fund, jointly owned by central government and participating councils. The fund would pay a approved installer to add batteries or solar panels to a home and then property owner would repay the fund at low interest rates over a ten-year period. The loans would be secured against the value of the property, and available to ratepayers with at least 20% equity in their property. The loans could be used for solar installation, batteries, heat pumps, insulation and other developments to make homes more efficient.

citations.title: 'Home Energy Fund', undated (accessed 10 September 2026)

policies.statement: Offer government backed long-term loans for home batteries and solar installations

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that energy security should be a priority for NZ, and it should be easy for businesses, households and farms to electrify. Changing planning processes to make it possible to install solar panels and batteries increases independence and resilience in the energy system and reduces power bills.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would allow property owners to install rooftop solar without a consent, regardless of regulations around height limits or landscape overlays. Battery installation not enclosed by an existing building would also be allowed as a property right, and there would be standard rules to govern any safety issues or other concerns about this. This would be part of other changes in the replacement for the current Resource Management Act.

citations.title: 'Home Energy Fund', undated (accessed 10 September 2026)
'Building the future: our plan to Electrify NZ' (PDF), undated (accessed 14 September 2026)

policies.statement: Allow rooftop solar and battery installation without a consent

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that small battery, solar and hydro projects have confusing regulations, making it hard for users like farmers to use natural resources on their own land. From the perspective of energy resilience and affordability, there should be standard and predictable rules so that it is easier for more people to build energy projects on their property. Small-scale renewables are a huge opportunity which New Zealanders should be able to take advantage of.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would permit on-farm mounted solar panels with clear and consistent rules around the country, including safeguards to protect environmentally important land and manage other effects. Small run-of-river hydro projects would be allowed for generating energy used on site, as long as the project is below a certain size and has acomadations for fish passage, water flow and other river users.

citations.title: 'Home Energy Fund', undated (accessed 10 September 2026)
'Building the future: our plan to Electrify NZ' (PDF), undated (accessed 14 September 2026)

policies.statement: Create standard rules for on-site small solar and hydro energy projects

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that NZ law does not define what consent is, but instead says what consent is not. This means that for legal purposes, the absence of a person saying "no" can be considered consent, depending on the circumstance. To create a better system for the victims of sexual offending, and to be in line with other jurisdictions, the definition of consent should be specified in the law.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would amend the Crimes Act to specify that consent must be actively given, whether through words or actions. Consent is also not permanent; consent given at one point in time, for one action, is not consent for all future actions. The prosecution would still need to prove beyond reasonable doubt that consent wasn't given, and that the defendant didn't believe, on reasonable grounds, that it was.

citations.title: 'Modernise sexual consent laws', undated (accessed 10 September 2026)

policies.statement: Specify that an active "yes" is required in laws around sexual consent

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that crime should have real consequences. A "good character" assessment can be a factor in receiving sentencing discounts for sexual offending.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would prohibit judges from using "good character" assessments as a mitigating factor for any sexual offending.

citations.title: 'Modernise sexual consent laws', undated (accessed 10 September 2026)
'Tougher Sentences', undated (accessed 10 September 2026)

policies.statement: Prevent "good character" from being a mitigating factor in sentencing for sexual offending

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that as Aucklanders get used to the City Rail Link, more people will be using public transport. Visible police officers help prevent offending. Taking public transport should feel safe, and having a police unit dedicated to Auckland's trains and buses will be good for all travellers.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would create an Auckland Transport Police Team, which would operate across Auckland's public transport network, on vehicles as well as at transport stations and hubs. This would require an addition 50 sworn officers, and would be funded with an additional $7m to the police in the 2027 Budget.  This party estimates that this policy would cost $7m from 2027.

citations.title: 'More Police on the beat, and on the bus', 13 September 2026 (accessed 14 September 2026)

policies.statement: Create a dedicated police team for Auckland public transport

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that Foodstuffs owns three grocery brands, limiting competition on prices in NZ. Previous attempts to reform the sector have suggested targeting both Woolworths and Foodstuffs, but a cost-benefit analysis says only focusing on Foodstuffs is the better option. Instead of Foodstuffs being divided into North and South Island branches, the company should be divided into New World and Four Square and Pak 'n' Save, creating greater competition.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would amend the Grocery Industry Competition Act in its first 100 days in government, asking the Commerce Commission to develop an implementation plan for separating the businesses in a way that is good for consumers. Owner-operators of supermarkets would retain their roles, but with a different overarching company structure to get support from. Restructuring Foodstuffs is a faster way to reach three competitors in the New Zealand market, rather than the time it would take for another player to develop operations around the country.

citations.title: 'More Grocery competition' (PDF), 16 September 2026 (accessed 17 September 2026)
'National to pursue separation of Foodstuffs', 16 September 2026 (accessed 16 September 2026)

policies.statement: Separate the Foodstuffs business into two nationwide cooperatives

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that it should be easier for large commercial projects to be built in New Zealand without needing a council inspection. Councils do not always have the capacity or expertise to sign off on large and complex projects, creating delays. Making it possible for engineers to sign off on parts of projects will reduce council inspections for parts of construction. Council capacity could be dedicated to consents and management of housing, and mean large projects could be built more quickly and cheaply.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would allow qualified engineers to sign off on building work by clarifying the role of producer statements in the Building Act, giving these descriptions a standard role in consent processes. It would also create a dedicated dedicated Building Consent Authority for large commercial projects, with specialist expertise and a nationally consistent pathway for consents. Developers could choose to use this BCA or get approval from their local council.

citations.title: 'National to make it easier to build the future', undated (accessed 10 September 2026)

policies.statement: Create a dedicated Building Consent Authority for large commercial buildings

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that evidence says there needs to be caution around screen use in young children. For early childhood education, there should be no screen use at all, while the use of digital technology in the first three years of primary school should be strictly limited. Technology should only be used to enhance education, rather than being the main way that kids learn. Instead, the focus should be on hands-on learning and interaction.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would end all screen use and individual device use in early childhood education settings. Screen use in Years 1 to 3 would be strictly limited, and age-appropriate restrictions would be placed on screen use for older primary aged students.

citations.title: 'Screen use to end in ECE and limits set in primary', 20 September 2026 (accessed 21 September 2026)

policies.statement: Limit the use of screens in school for primary-aged and younger children

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says children need to be ready for school, and parents and teachers need to be aware of developmental milestones. Skills like toilet training, holding pencils and scissors, and eating independently are important for kids to thrive as they start school. A checklist of expectations for starting school will help teachers and parents know when a child might need extra support to be prepared for being at school all day. This would formalise a process many ECE centres already have.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would create a "School Start Check" for use by ECE centres and parents. The expectations for transitioning to primary school would be clear, and kids struggling to meet these expectations would be given extra support. The checklist would not be a "pass/fail" test, and not completing the checklist would not prevent a child from starting school.

citations.title: 'Screen use to end in ECE and limits set in primary', 20 September 2026 (accessed 21 September 2026)

policies.statement: Use a checklist in early childhood settings to assess school readiness

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that primary-age education should be focused on books, handwriting, conversation and in-person interaction, not digital technology and screens. Evidence shows that writing by hand when learning to write and read helps children retain information.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would require that students complete the writing component of twice-yearly primary school assessments on paper, by hand, rather than on computers.

citations.title: 'Screen use to end in ECE and limits set in primary', 20 September 2026 (accessed 21 September 2026)

policies.statement: Require primary school writing assessments to be completed on paper

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that older New Zealanders need the balance in relationships with retirement village companies to shift more towards residents. Residents and families need certainty about when money will arrive when they no longer occupy a unit. While some have called for a three month repayment deadline, it says that modelling shows that this would add up to about $118,000 to the cost of entering a village if all expenses were passed to residents.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would require retirement villages to pay residents or their families 10 percent of their net termination proceeds within four weeks of when they leave a unit. The maximum amount of time that villages could take to repay residents or families would be shortened to nine months. It would retain the current "hardship pathway" and current exit protections for residents, like stopping weekly fees when a occupation agreement ends. The 10 percent upfront payment requirement will not apply to villages with fewer than 50 units.

citations.title: 'Faster and fairer retirement village repayments', 18 September 2026 (accessed 21 September 2026)

policies.statement: Require retirement villages to pay out house sales within nine months

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that firefighters fulfil a vital role in the community, but are stymied by organisational structures, unreliable equipment and lack of support for volunteers. The FENZ board is a Crown agent and reports to the Internal Affairs minister; with concerns about the organisational structure and gaps in training, it says reform in needed urgently.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would remove the FENZ board and reorganise it as a government agency, directly accountable to the minister for emergeny management. FENZ would be required to write the turnaround plan and cover costs from existing baselines.

citations.title: 'National’s plan to back our firefighters', 23 September 2026 (accessed 24 September 2026)

policies.statement: Change the structure of Fire and Emergency New Zealand

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that firefighters fill a vital role serving the public, despite faulty appliances. Volunteers work in fire response around the country, but though this is risky work and requires extensive training, these volunteers need more support, beyond what is already covered by ACC. It says that for volunteer and professional firefighters alike, investment in equipment will make their work safer and more effective, as currently many of their tools are not fit for purpose.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would require FENZ to provide private insurance covering mental injury and gradual process injuries for operational volunteers. It would direct FENZ to create a fleet management plan which could be used to secure production slots in advance for equipment that needs replacement. It would also ask for a plan that would allow all recruits to get experience on live fires during training, modernise axle mass rules, ensure all Type 3, 5 and 6 appliances are delivered, accepted, and put into operational use and prioritise capability over emissions profiles for frontline vehicles.

citations.title: 'National’s plan to back our firefighters', 23 September 2026 (accessed 24 September 2026)

policies.statement: Increase funding for volunteers and frontline work at Fire and Emergency NZ

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that financial investment is required for growth. It should be easier for businesses to invest across borders, especially as global fuel shocks push up prices.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would double the threshold for shares of overseas businesses to be required to follow the foreign investment fund rules.

citations.title: 'National's Economic Plan' (PDF), undated (accessed 30 September 2026)

policies.statement: Increase the threshold for shares to be declared due to foreign investment rules

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that businesses create wealth, not governments. Businesses need opportunities to grow, no matter what stage they are at. As well as reducing other regulations like resource management, businesses should be able to compete for government contracts. Currently, the government purchases more than $50bn of services and goods from businesses each year.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would open current supplier panels for government contracts so that more businesses can bid to be suppliers. It says that this would increase competition.

citations.title: 'National's Economic Plan' (PDF), undated (accessed 30 September 2026)

policies.statement: Open supplier panels for government procurement

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that the government should do everything it can to make it easier to build, invest, hire and export, and help businesses grow in general. Making it easier to comply with health and safety law will make it easier for businesses to succeed.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would rewrite health and safety codes in simple, plain language to make it easier for businesses to comply with these regulations.

citations.title: 'National's Economic Plan' (PDF), undated (accessed 30 September 2026)

policies.statement: Rewrite industry health and safety codes in simple language

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that NZ needs to support new technologies and businesses that create new jobs. Complex systems of regulations and consents should be simplified so that there is less bureaucracy.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would co-ordinate regulations across the Reserve Bank, Financial Markets Authority and MBIE to remove barriers impacting the introduction of new financial technologies.

citations.title: 'National's Economic Plan' (PDF), undated (accessed 30 September 2026)
'National’s Economic Plan backs Kiwis to get ahead', 28 September 2026 (accessed 30 September 2026)

policies.statement: Coordinate regulation for new financial technology businesses

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that NZ's growth and prosperity depends on the knowledge and skills of young people. However, some employers have been struggling to find the skills they need.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would double the number of Trades Academy places so that 20,000 places are offered by 2030.  It would also roll out 9 new vocational education pathways designed by industry.

citations.title: 'National's Economic Plan' (PDF), undated (accessed 30 September 2026)

policies.statement: Double the number of Trade Academy places by 2030

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that NZ's achievement in maths, reading and writing has decreased. Structured literacy and maths and a simple grading system and regular assessment is a way to create better outcomes. A new curriculum should be used at all year levels.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would replace the NCEA system with grades and regular exams. Grades would range from A+ to E, rather than the NCEA system. New curriculums would be fully embedded at all levels.

citations.title: 'National’s Economic Plan backs Kiwis to get ahead', 28 September 2026 (accessed 30 September 2026)
'National's Economic Plan' (PDF), undated (accessed 30 September 2026)

policies.statement: Replace NCEA with a different grading system

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that NZ needs partners on the world stage to help businesses get ahead. People from other countries with money to spend should be encouraged to stay and invest in NZ with the Active Investor Plus visa categories. Investment fund settings and IRD rules should not prevent them from doing so.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would ensure that IRD rules and investment fund settings do not discourage Active Investor Plus visa holders. These visa holders must have at least $5m or $10m to invest in New Zealand to meet the visa rules.

citations.title: 'National's Economic Plan' (PDF), undated (accessed 30 September 2026)
'National’s Economic Plan backs Kiwis to get ahead', 28 September 2026 (accessed 30 September 2026)

'Active Investor Plus delivers $3 billion in investment in New Zealand
', 13 February 2026 (accessed 01 October 2026)

policies.statement: Encourage Active Investor Plus visa holders to stay in New Zealand

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that infrastructure is a priority, especially because NZ has an infrastructure deficit. It should be cheaper to build needed infrastructure in NZ, including needed roads. This party has identified a list of Roads of National Significance, which are roads it will invest in creating or upgrading.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would begin construction of the Cambridge to Piare Road and the Northern Expressway by early 2027.

citations.title: 'National's Economic Plan' (PDF), undated (accessed 30 September 2026)
'National’s Economic Plan backs Kiwis to get ahead', 28 September 2026 (accessed 30 September 2026)
'Mill Road Stage One given the green light', 4 October 2026 (accessed 06 October 2026)

policies.statement: Complete construction on the next set of Roads of National Significance

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that NZ has an infrastructure deficit, and replacements are needed to key pieces of infrastructure like schools, roads and hospitals. This infrastructure should be built affordably without using an inappropriate amount of taxpayer's money. Infrastructure built by government and councils should be managed carefully with asset and capital plans.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would require the Infrastructure Commission to use international cost-benchmarks for government funded builds of infrastructure like schools, transport and hospitals. It would also legislate requirements for asset management and long-term capital plans.

citations.title: 'National's Economic Plan' (PDF), undated (accessed 30 September 2026)

policies.statement: Require government infrastructure builds to use internationally cost benchmarks

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that NZ and Australia are two of the world's most closely connected economies. Citizens of both countries can already use "smart gates" to enter the country without interacting with a border agent. In 2028 NZ and Australia are jointly hosting the Cricket World Cup, which is an opportunity to trial a way to enter the country without needing a paper passport at all.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would introduce a "seamless" digital system for travelling between New Zealand and Australia, to be trialled before the 2028 World Cup. To do this, NZ and Australian officials would work together to design the system. It would use a smartphone, digital credentials and biometric technology to identify people at the border, rather than a physical passport.

citations.title: 'National to trial seamless trans-Tasman travel', 1 October 2026 (accessed 01 October 2026)

policies.statement: Trial digital-first "seamless" travel between NZ and Australia

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that secure energy is important for NZ to grow its economy. More power supply, competition and choice, as well as regulating the right areas, can make power cheaper for New Zealanders.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would change the law so that "affordability" is a key objective for the Electricity Authority in its role as the sector regulator. Affordability would be balanced with its other objectives of competition, reliability and efficiency.

citations.title: 'Electrify NZ 2.0 ' (PDF), undated (accessed 02 October 2026)

policies.statement: Legislate affordability as a concern of the Electricity Authority

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that affordable and reliable power is essential for growing the economy. However, some of the areas with possibility for new development of wind, solar and geothermal power generation do not have enough transmission capacity. The system of treating transmission as an asset means that one party might pay for building transmission that benefits multiple power companies and developers.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would amend the Electricity Act and revise the Industry Participation Code so transmission pricing methodology can recover the costs of investments made by parties other than Transpower. Privately funded interconnection investments would be required to use the same pricing method as well. To encourage private investment, there would be a regulatory framework for connecting private transmission to the main grid operated by Transpower.

citations.title: 'Electrify NZ 2.0 ' (PDF), undated (accessed 02 October 2026)

policies.statement: Make the cost of building transmission for new electricity generation consistent for public and private players

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that connecting a new new home, subdivision, farm, factory or business to the electricity network is often slow and expensive. Customers have little choice in the work, as it is set and priced by the network authority. This area of the electricity industry should be more competitive.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would establish a single accreditation scheme for connection contractors, which would be independently assessed. Accredited contractors would be allowed to work on any network in the country. People seeking a connection could get quotes for the work from multiple people. Networks would still be allowed to inspect finished work and approve designs, but would be given set timelines for doing so.

citations.title: 'Electrify NZ 2.0 ' (PDF), undated (accessed 02 October 2026)

policies.statement: Create a single accreditation scheme for power to new developments or houses

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that NZ uses largely renewable electricity, which is cheap and abundant. However, this power, especially hydro power, can be unreliable when there is a dry spell and the hydro lakes are low. Back-up has historically been provided by gas, but gas stocks are decreasing. As well as a contract for daily peaks, the 4 big power generators should have a contract for covering gaps over the weeks or months of a dry period.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would require the Electricity Authority to publish a report about the "back-up gap" with the size and timing of generation that is not covered. Along with published data on contract values, lengths and price ranges, this would help electricity buyers, sellers and investors know what is happening. It would require the creation of a back-up contract so that back-up power can be bought by anyone from any retailer on standardised terms. There would be regular auctions for this contract.

citations.title: 'Electrify NZ 2.0 ' (PDF), undated (accessed 02 October 2026)
'Affordable Power Kiwis can rely on ', 2 October 2026 (accessed 02 October 2026)

policies.statement: Create a back-up power contract for dry years

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that network charges are responsible for 2/3 of the price increases in power over the past year. This is partially because lines companies charges are set by an independent regulator and the current cap was set in November 2024 when inflation was high. It was designed for a system before solar power, as houses and businesses can now generate as well as consume power.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would review part 4 of the Commerce Act regarding electricity distribution to see whether the current system is delivering enough value for money for consumers. It would require distribution businesses to approve residential and small business solar connection applications within two working days, with penalties for lateness.

citations.title: 'Electrify NZ 2.0 ' (PDF), undated (accessed 02 October 2026)

policies.statement: Review the system that sets electricity lines charges

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that the current rules in the electricity sector assumes that power comes from big generators. However, as more people put solar panels on their homes or businesses, the power sometimes flows the other way. Currently, those with solar panels are locked into selling any excess power to the grid to the same company they have an electricity contract with. If these rules were more flexible, people could get a better price for power they generate.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would give every household and. business the right to sell power to whichever retailer they choose. This would be achieved through a Government Policy Statement, and specific legislation if needed. Lines companies would be required to base any power export limits on the true capacity of their network, and not restrict exports beyond any genuine network constraint.

citations.title: 'Electrify NZ 2.0 ' (PDF), undated (accessed 02 October 2026)

policies.statement: Allow people with solar generation to sell power to any buyer

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that Canterbury is the engine room of the South Island, with State Highway 1 already carrying 21,500 vehicles a day. This is predicted to grow to around 28,000 vehicles a day by 2048, with Woodend feeling the peak pressure, amid other safety concerns. This project will create a reliable and safe transport corridor for people and freight travelling and commuting each day.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would fully fund an extension to the Christchurch Northern Motorway for $800 million, which would be allocated in next year's budget. This incorporates the Belfast to Pegasus Motorway and Woodend Bypass.

citations.title: 'National promises to fund $800 million Christchurch Northern Motorway extension', 5 October 2026 (accessed 06 October 2026)

policies.statement: Fund $800 million Christchurch Northern Motorway extension

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that this funding boost will expand access to new cancer and other life-saving medicines so Kiwis can access world-class treatment here in New Zealand.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would deliver a further $604 million uplift in Pharmac’s medicines budget. This will be funded by reducing foreign aid spent outside the Pacific.

citations.title: 'More medicines and earlier care', 6 October 2026 (accessed 06 October 2026)
'Building the Future: More medicines and earlier care' (PDF), 6 October 2026 (accessed 06 October 2026)

policies.statement: Increase funding for Pharmac's medicines budget

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that a national clinical trials target will mean that Kiwis can access the newest treatments sooner, accessing life-saving care. This matters even more for people living with a rare disorder, where so few treatments are funded that a trial can be one of the only options available.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would set a national target that within ten years, 5 percent of New Zealanders being treated for cancer will have part of their care delivered through a clinical trial, where a trial is right for them and they want to take part, aligning with Australia. It would also set up a single national front door for clinical trials, so companies have one clear place to go and patients can be matched to trials more easily, including those with a rare disorder who often struggle to find a relevant study. Lastly, it would simplify and standardise the approvals process, so a trial approved once can run right across the country, while keeping strong protections for patient safety.

citations.title: 'More medicines and earlier care', 6 October 2026 (accessed 06 October 2026)
'Building the Future: More medicines and earlier care' (PDF), 6 October 2026 (accessed 06 October 2026)

policies.statement: Set a national target for clinical trials

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that New Zealanders who need this life-saving technology currently rely on their cells being sent overseas to be made. This comes with a huge expense, despite scientists and clinicians who know how to do this already living here in New Zealand.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would co-invest $25 million with the BioOra company to expand its cell therapy manufacturing, research, and clinical facilities in Christchurch, so Kiwis who need CAR-T can be treated at home rather than sent overseas. BioOra is a New Zealand-based commercial-stage biotechnology company.

citations.title: 'More medicines and earlier care', 6 October 2026 (accessed 06 October 2026)
'Building the Future: More medicines and earlier care' (PDF), 6 October 2026 (accessed 06 October 2026)

policies.statement: Unlock CAR-T cell therapy for cancer patients by funding BioOra

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that New Zealand's rate of bowel cancer is among the highest in the world, with more than 3300 people diagnosed every year and 1200 losing their lives to it. Early detection is the difference between survival and death. Those treated at an early stage have a 90 percent chance of long-term survival.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would extend free bowel screening by lowering the age by two years every year to reach 50 in the next term of Government, so bowel cancer is found earlier when it is most treatable. It would continue the roll out of free bowel cancer tests for people of any age with symptoms, so cancer is found sooner no matter how old a patient is. Lastly, it would deliver additional colonoscopies to increase system capacity and work with Bowel Cancer New Zealand to determine how the CHALLENGE exercise programme could be made available for bowel cancer patients.

citations.title: 'More medicines and earlier care', 6 October 2026 (accessed 06 October 2026)
'Building the Future: More medicines and earlier care' (PDF), 6 October 2026 (accessed 06 October 2026)

policies.statement: Lower the free bowel screening age to 50 by 2029

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that breast cancer is New Zealand’s most commonly diagnosed cancer in women, with nearly 3900 new cases a year, and the risk grows with age. Free mammograms currently stop at 69, leaving older women to pay for screening themselves or go without.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would complete the free breast screening extension to age 74 by 2029, ensuring older women have access to early detection and life-saving care.

citations.title: 'More medicines and earlier care', 6 October 2026 (accessed 06 October 2026)
'Building the Future: More medicines and earlier care' (PDF), 6 October 2026 (accessed 06 October 2026)

policies.statement: Extend free breast screening extension to age 74 by 2029

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that prostate cancer is the most common cancer among New Zealand men, with more than 4,000 diagnosed and more than 700 deaths each year, making it the second biggest cause of cancer death for men after lung cancer. Found early, more than 90 per cent of men survive at least five years, but that falls below 40 per cent once the cancer has spread. However, there is currently no organised screening programme for prostate cancer.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would launch a prostate cancer screening pilot in two high-demand districts, offering men aged 50 to 70 regular screening to evaluate what works for a potential nationwide programme. It would also gather evidence for a potential nationwide programme, based on a proposal from the Prostate Cancer Foundation.

attributes.value: This party says that cervical cancer is among the most preventable cancers, because nearly every case is caused by HPV, a common virus that the screening test picks up well before any cancer develops. When it is caught early, around 91 percent of women survive, but that falls to around 19 percent once it has spread. Successive Parliamentary Reviews since 2018 have recommended making cervical screening free for every woman.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would deliver free cervical screening for all women aged 25 to 69 from March 2027.

attributes.value: This party says that New Zealand is facing a chronic disease epidemic. The number of Kiwis with type 2 diabetes is set to nearly double by 2040, yet most cases are preventable with a healthy diet and exercise.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would establish the Healthy Kiwis Programme to deliver active prescriptions, with a target to double the number of people receiving them by 2030, helping more Kiwis get active, eat well, and avoid chronic diseases like diabetes.

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that lung cancer is New Zealand’s biggest cancer killer, claiming more than 1700 lives every year. However, most people are only diagnosed once the disease is advanced, and the chance of a cure is slim. Screening can change this. International trials have found that low-dose CT scans for people at high risk reduce lung cancer deaths by 20 to 25 per cent.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would deliver a lung cancer screening pilot in Bay of Plenty and Hawke’s Bay, offering low-dose CT scans to people at high risk, such as current and former smokers. The pilot will test the best way to find, invite, and screen those most at risk, catching more lung cancers early and building the evidence for a potential nationwide programme.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would introduce a First Employee Support Package with practical first-year guidance and reduced penalties for genuine administrative mistakes. This will deliver practical, dedicated advice for new employers through the first year of their first hire - including employment agreement tools, payroll guidance, and tax and ACC reminders.

attributes.value: This party says that changing a business address or contact details should be straightforward. Owners should not have to waste their time working through a list of agencies updating the same information in different systems.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would deliver a 'Tell Government Once' service built around the New Zealand Business Number and existing government systems, including Inland Revenue, ACC, the Companies Office and relevant licensing bodies. This will mean core business information can be updated once and shared across participating agencies and councils. It would also explore integrating this service with Councils. There would be clear privacy rules and business control over the information shared.

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that Jobseeker benefits are not meant as long-term support. The current "invest to save" programme should be continued and extended, with work support targeted to people who have been receiving a benefit for a longer period of time. More intense case management and employment programmes should be used to target the problems preventing people from being employed, and younger people should particularly receive more help. This will help to balance the welfare system more effectively.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would target extra case management and employment programmes to people receiving Jobseeker benefits for over 12 months, who are deemed "job-ready". At least 5,000 of these places would be reserved for young people. An additional $12m would be given to youth work programme He Poutama Rangatahi above existing baselines. It is estimated that this programme would save $9m by 2031.

policies.statement: Provide targeted work support to 30,000 Jobseekers

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that welfare support should always be temporary, and after a long time receiving a benefit it is hard for people to find work. While the welfare system should provide a safety net, it should not prevent people from seeking work. Decreasing payments for people who have been receiving benefits for more than two years will incentivise these people to seek work. Parents with dependent children would have their payments decreased less than those without children.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would reduce payments for people who have been receiving Jobseeker benefits for 2 of the last 3 years, even if these periods of support were not consecutive. From April 2028, this party would reduce the rate for single people to the rate for 20-24 year olds; reduce the rate for couples without children, and reduce the Jobseeker rate for parents with dependent children half as much as for those without. The exact reductions would be based on benefit rates in 2028, as the rate changes with inflation. The Supported Living payment would not change. This party estimates this would save $572m over 4 years.

policies.statement: Reduce benefit payments for people receiving support for more than 2 years

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that the intention of Jobseeker benefits is to help people find work, not to provide long-term support. Many types of work require drug tests for workers, so people receiving Jobseeker benefits should also be tested for drugs, to show that they are ready to work. If drug use is a barrier to employment, it should be addressed.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would institute random drug tests for people on Jobseeker benefits, as part of MSD's broader employment programme. If drugs are detected, a person will be tested again; if drugs are detected again, MSD will conduct a mandatory assessment to see whether drug use is a barrier to employment and whether it should be addressed. If drug use if not addressed, it could result in benefit sanctions, so that payments are reduced or stopped. It is expected that this policy would cost $1.5m per year.

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that benefits are intended as temporary support until someone is employed again. If someone chooses to leave a job, the current stand-down period of 13 weeks means they cannot receive a benefit for job hunting until this time has passed. In line with the UK's benefit sanctions system, people who repeatedly leave jobs should have a longer stand-down period.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would increase the current non-entitlement period for people who leave a job from 13 weeks to 26 weeks. Someone who has left a job more than once would not receive a benefit until this time, about 6 months, had passed.

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that NZ's welfare system is funded by taxpayers to provide a safety net. Currently, NZ residents are entitled to benefits after 2 years of living in the country. However, this party says that new migrants to NZ should be expected to provide for themselves and their families by working rather than receiving benefits. This is in line with approaches to new residents in Australia and the UK.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would extend the minimum residency requirements for receiving benefits to 5 years, from the current minimum of 2 years. This would begin in 2028, and new legislation might be needed to enact the change. Refugees and other protected persons would be exempt from this requirement and MSD could still issue hardship grants to residents in emergencies. This party estimates that this would save $49m over 4 years.

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that water supports agriculture in New Zealand, creating regional jobs and export earnings. While New Zealand receives some of the most rainfall of anywhere in the world, many regions still have water shortages. Water storage on farms can make it more consistent for farmers throughout the year. An additional 400,000 hectares are ready to be cultivated if there is enough irrigation.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would publish a National Rural and Provincial Water Use Strategy in 2027 with a storage register. It would also create a National Standard for on-farm and lower risk "off-stream" water storage. There would also be a National Standard for irrigation so that consenting for new irrigation uses was more straightforward.

policies.statement: Introduce a National Standard for irrigation and water storage

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that water is essential for NZ agriculture, but only about 2 percent of NZ rainwater is used as irrigation. Despite this, many regions face water shortages. It says that enabling more water storage infrastructure will help the agriculture industry and retain rural jobs.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would commit $300m of concessional loans for building water storage, starting with 5 priority projects. It would work with iwi, councils, growers and farmers to create a National Rural and Provincial Water Use Strategy in 2027.

attributes.value: This party says that small businesses need to be paid promptly for effective cashflow, especially when they are working for government. Building on current reforms, government agencies should be accountable for how quickly they pay invoices and digital invoicing should be used to make processes simpler. Lowering payment fees could help small businesses by reducing costs.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would hold Government agencies to account for delayed payment by publishing how quickly agencies pay invoices. It would monitor whether fee reductions reach businesses and expand the use of eInvoicing. Open banking and the Reserve Bank's payment modernisation programme would be completed and fair payment terms through supply chains would be enforced.

This party would offer more places on this pilot programme.

attributes.value: This party would fund another 120 places in the AI Advisory pilot programme. It would continue to co-fund support for some small businesses to do AI courses and receive expert input.

attributes.value: This party says that many NZ small businesses want to export their goods but do not have the time or expertise to navigate complex export processes. It should be easier to export NZ products offshore, and AI tools and trade agreements can facilitate this.

It would expand "paperless" trade with real-time electronic certification when exporting to close trading partners like the UK. It says there should be more consolidation in regulations which impact consenting.

attributes.value: This party would cut project information memorandum processing times from 20 to 10 working days and require regulators to reuse engineering and geotechnical reports if they are still relevant and fit for purpose. It would expand the list of overseas-certified products which could be used in buildings in NZ. It would change building indemnity insurance so it is proportionate to the building and enable greater consolidation in the building-consent regime more broadly.

attributes.value: This party says that many businesses serve their customers online and requirements to use faxes or publish newspaper notices feel obsolete. Wherever possible, secure and consistent digital systems should be used instead of paper alternatives.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would remove unjustified "paper retention" policies and create guidelines for accepting paper alternatives. It would remove licence display requirements when there are accessible digital alternatives. This party would replace compulsory newspaper notices with a searchable online gazette and remove fax and telex requirements, which are obsolete.

attributes.value: This party would align renewal dates for licences where possible and introduce automatic renewals for low-risk businesses with strong compliance records. attributes.value: This party says that currently, unions can begin collective bargaining without a minimum number of employees supporting the action. There should be a minimum number or percentage of employees in support of bargaining for a collective agreement process to take place. It says this is in line with similar laws in the UK.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would require support from 10 employees or 20 percent of a workplace, whichever is lesser, before collective bargaining over wages or working conditions can take place. The minimum number of employees would be two.

policies.statement: Increase employee support requirements for collective bargaining

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that employment disputes can be expensive and time-consuming, even if a dispute is relatively minor. For the peace of mind, costs, and time involved for employer and employees, it should be easier, faster, and cheaper to go through an employment dispute. Changes should particularly focus on the Employment Relations Authority, and on mediation so cases do not reach the Authority and are resolved more easily.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value:
This party would create a fast-track through the Employment Relations Authority for minor disputes, and allow a greater role for mediators, with binding agreements clearly explained to all parties. It would require Employment Relations Authority decisions within one month of final submissions. 
To increase transparency, this party would create a process for tracking a case through the Authority's system and require the Authority to record and reuse oral evidence when legal and suitable, to prevent multiple submissions of the same evidence. It would review the Employment Relations Authority’s enforcement powers (especially where it engages with other courts) and regulate paid employment advocates with standards of conduct and information about fees.

attributes.value: This party says that NZ employment law is spread across many different frameworks, laws, and statutes. This makes it particularly hard for small businesses to comply with a wide variety of rules. By consolidating different employment rules, this party says employment regulations would be easier to navigate.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would progress a Employment Relations Consolidation Bill in Parliament, with the focus of the legislation making the law easier to navigate with minimal cross-references. It would also clarify part of the Employment Relations Act to clarify when a contractor becomes an employee so that both parties know which laws apply before a dispute process begins.

This party says the threshold should be reviewed to see if it is still appropriate.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would commission a review of the GST threshold, focused on barriers to compliance and considering the fiscal cost of any change.

This party says there should be a specific process for hiring recurring workers for seasonal work.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would develop a standard recurring seasonal agreement and a short renewal process for seasonal employers to use, meaning dates have to be changed but less paperwork is required.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would work with training providers to ensure approved digital competency records and electronic supervisor sign-off are consistently accepted across apprenticeships.

attributes.value: This party says that currently students are allowed to leave school once they are 16, which means that in many cases students do not complete Year 11. With curriculum updates requiring English and maths learning until the end of Year 11, it is important students complete the year and gain these useful skills before entering the workforce.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would require students to complete Year 11 or turn 16 before leaving school, whichever is later. This party would also use a Foundational Award in literacy and numeracy for students who finish the year. Students would still be able to apply for a leaving exemption earlier if they had found a job or were moving into further training.

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that the Hauraki Gulf is a special area and "Auckland's playground". It believes that the waters of the Gulf are best used by people who fish, dive, swim, or collect kaimoana recreationally. Further protection for the Gulf will preserve these recreational uses.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would establish the Hākaimangō-Matiatia Marine Reserve off Waiheke Island as a 23 square km marine reserve, and expand the size of the existing Goat Island marine reserve. It would remove the exemption for ringnet fishing in the High Protection Areas of the Gulf. The current ban on collecting shellfish and other species from rockpools would be maintained and this party would impose higher penalties and enforce this ban more strictly. It would develop a Sustainable Fisheries Plan for the Hauraki Gulf by consulting with industry, including reviewing the current corridors where bottom trawling is allowed.

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that at least 600,000 New Zealanders go fishing occasionally, and recreational fish provides food and enjoyment, as well as supporting the business of charter boat tourism for fishing access. Fish stocks need to be maintained for recreational users, but fishing for food is a right and should not require a licence. This party says that honorary Fisheries Officers, who do enforcement work on a voluntary basis, could be doing more of the work of fisheries enforcement.

Enforcement and fines for people who do not obey catch limits would be increased, and part of this enforcement would be carried out by increasing the number of Honorary Fisheries Officers to 200 around the country. There would be some instant fines for people who catch more than the limit of fish.

attributes.value: This party says that New Zealand has over 1900 seamounts (mountains and hills on the ocean floor which often have more biodiversity) in its Exclusive Economic Zone (the area of ocean which a country has the right to resources within). Protecting these areas is important, as is following the Crown's obligations under the Fisheries Settlement of Te Tiriti. It says better data can protect this area while also maintaining access for recreational and commercial fishing.

More broadly, this party would continue to uphold the government's obligations to protect fisheries under Te Tiriti o Waitangi.

party.description: The NZ Loyal Party is a far-right party. Founded in 2023 by antivax activist Liz Gunn, the party’s program revolves around opposition to ‘globalist’ institutions such as the United Nations, Banks, and the World Economic Forum. It opposes both immigration and taxation. The party is currently led by far-right activist Kelvyn Alp. He has a background in conspiracy media, an armed militia that has targeted bankers, and has been involved in legal battles regarding the distribution of videos from the Christchurch Mosque attacks. It has never won a seat in parliament.

party.description: Opportunity, formerly known as the Opportunity Party, is a radical centrist party. Its program has emphasised a combination of economic efficiency, environmental concerns and well-being. Founded in 2016 by businessman and philanthropist Gareth Morgen with the intention of having a party that can work with both sides based on empirical evidence. It has yet to enter parliament, and its best election result was in 2017 when it received 2.4% percent or 63,261 votes. Opportunity is led by Quilae Wong, whose background is sustainable business consulting at KPMG.

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that the current tax system is outdated and does not address the cost-of-living crisis, unaffordable housing, and the increasing pressure of the superannuation system. Under its tax plan, this party says incomes will increase for 70 percent of New Zealanders, and another 20% will see no change.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value:
An annual land value tax of 1.75 percent on urban land - and 0.5% on rural land - would be part of a wider tax reset aimed at incomes, house prices and retirement savings. The land value tax would lower house prices an estimated 10-15 percent and discourage land-banking and large property portfolios. There would be potential exemptions for farmers, retirees and other "land rich, cash poor" land owners. 
This tax would fund a universal citizen's income, with an extra $4bn for other uses. The tax system would also be simplified, with the number of tax brackets reduced to three - 28 percent, 34 percent and 39 percent

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says the seas are hitting their ecological and economic limits. Fish species are being depleted under the current quota management system, and critical habitats are unprotected. Just 0.5 percent of NZ’s extensive ocean territory is protected as a marine reserve.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value:
This party would increase NZ's marine reserves to 30% of its ocean territory by 2035 and replace the Marine Reserves Act 1971. The party also aims to deliver at least 10,000 hectares of restored coastal habitat.  It would also establish integrated ocean governance through a reinstated Ocean Secretariat.
These moves fit within a wider ocean policy. The short-term cost is expected to be no more than $100m a year, some of which would be recovered from the commercial fishing industry.

attributes.value: This party says that there is broad agreement across science, industry, and government that the current gene technology framework is no longer fit for purpose. However, the current bill was developed without proper public consultation, leaving critical questions around trade, liability and environmental risk. The bill includes no clear statement obligating the regulator to protect people and the environment and no full regulatory impact statement. Left as it is, the party says the bill could create one of the most liberal gene technology regimes in the world.

It favours full industry and public consultation and backs a modern framework, based on independent expert assessment, case-by-case evaluation and accountability. It calls for a national conversation on gene technology.

attributes.value: This party says that New Zealand's education system is capable of excellence, but it has since become politicised and student results have fallen. attributes.value: This party says that our health system is under immense pressure because it changes whenever governments change, sacrificing long-term progress. People are finding it difficult to access care and the medical profession needs stability. Filling the gaps in primary care, Māori wellbeing, workforce, mental health, and elective treatment would cost at about $1.3b a year, or an additional 1.5 per cent of annual GDP.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would lift health funding from the current 7.4 per cent to 9 percent of GDP over the next 10 years. Funding for GPs and other primary care providers would also be increased to help catch illness early or even prevent it. This would rise gradually from 5.7 to 10 percent of Health NZ's spending. By setting health funding as a share of GDP, it will grow consistently with the economy, rather than having to be found each Budget.

attributes.value: This party says that electrification of industry is being blocked by the cost of plant capital, grid connection and network upgrades. party.description: Te Pāti Māori is a left-wing indigenous rights party. Its programme couples a larger role for the government in the economy alongside an emphasis on “for Māori-by-Māori” solutions and Māori self-determination. It was founded in 2004 by Tariana Turei as a breakaway from the Labour Party following the Foreshore and Seabed legislation that blocked Māori land claims. The party has been in government only once, from 2008 to 2014, in the fifth National government. It has regularly held Māori seats in Parliament and currently holds 4 of the 7 Māori seats.
party.name: Te Pāti Māori

The focus should be on dignity, care and support, not fighting a beureaucratic system.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would make support easier to access and reduce the focus on bureaucratic requirements. Funding would be provided based on what families say they need, not bureaucratic forms.

attributes.value: This party says that argues that Aotearoa's tax system is highly unequal, given that wages are taxed more than income from wealth. Lower-earning people have less disposable income; this party seeks to reduce how much this group is taxed.

attributes.value: This party would establish six bands of income tax. The first $30,000 earned would be tax-free, while income between $30,001 and $60,000 would have a tax rate of 15%. Those earning between $60,001 and $90,001 would have a tax rate of 33%; $ 90,001- $ 180,000 would be 39%; between $180,000 and $300,000, 42%; and above $300,000, the tax rate would be 48%.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would will create a Te Tiriti commission. The commission would investigate Crown activities which may breach Te Tiriti, report to Parliament on breaches, stop decisions or actions which breach Te Tiriti and require remedial action from the Crown when such breaches occur. The commission would use a Te Tiriti compliance order to prevent the government from continuing the activity. Such orders could only be overturned by the High Court.

The Mātike Mai project, which was founded in 2010 to strengthen the independence of iwi and hapū, is underfunded to resource such a transition.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would convene a Māori constitutional convention which will start dialogue with tangata Tiriti and both local and central government regarding New Zealand's constitutional future. It would set 2040 as a target date for constitutional change in New Zealand, and estimates that this policy would cost $220m. This would follow the recommendations of the Matike Mai report.

party.description: The Te Tai Tokerau Party is an electorate-focused indigenous rights party. It was founded in 2026 to support the candidacy of former Te Pati Māori and current MP Mariameno Kapa-Kingi. Kapa-Kingi was suspended by her party following accusations of mismanaging funds. She successfully challenged that suspension in the High Court. With a background in Iwi-run social services, Kapa-Kingi was most prominently the Te Pati Māori spokesperson for housing, children, and Oranga Tamariki.
party.name: Te Tai Tokerau Party

party.description: Vision New Zealand is a far-right Christian fundamentalist party. Its programme consists of promoting Christian family values, a smaller role for government, pausing immigration and taking conservative positions on indigenous rights. The party also holds positions opposing abortion, homosexuality, and the construction of new mosques. Founded in 2019 by Brian Tamaki and his wife, Hannah, who leads the party, Vision NZ has not won any seats in parliament. In 2023, it won 0.33% percent of the vote, under the umbrella of Freedoms New Zealand.
party.name: Vision NZ

party.description: The Women’s Rights Party is a trans-critical feminist political party. The party program emphasises that women’s rights are to be based on binary sex as opposed to gender identity. The party co-leaders are Jill Ovens and Dawn Trenberth. Ovens was a trade unionist and former president of the Alliance Party, while Trenberth, who had been a member of Labour, was also a trade unionist. The pair left the Labour Party in 2023, feeling alienated by increased hostility to trans-critical feminist perspectives. The Women’s Right’s Party was founded in 2023 and has never won a seat or entered parliament. In 2023, it received 0.08% percent, or 2,513 votes.
party.name: Women's Rights Party
